docs.title: A. New Lévy process (zoo/levy)
docs.text:
Open a Process Proposal issue first. The proposal must contain: 1. The Lévy–Khintchine triplet \((b, \sigma^2, \nu)\) in closed form, with derivation or citation 2. Cumulant formulas (at minimum \(\kappa_1\) and \(\kappa_2\)) with citation 3. The primary reference (original journal paper — not a textbook) 4. Proposed ExactnessLevel (must be EXACT for a Lévy process with known triplet) 5. The simulation algorithm with complexity per step

Files to create or modify:

1. Create spxa/zoo/levy/<name>.py

The file must contain:

# Module-level docstring with full mathematical specification:
# - Lévy density k(x)
# - Triplet (b, σ², ν)
# - Cumulant formulas
# - All primary references

def _<name>_levy_measure(params) -> DensityLevyMeasure:
    """
    Lévy density function.
    Cite the exact equation number and reference.
    """
    def density(x: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: ...
    def tail(xv: float) -> float: ...
    def moment_n() -> float: ...   # for each n you know exactly

    return DensityLevyMeasure(
        _density_fn=density,
        _total_mass=np.inf,        # or finite for compound Poisson
        _tail_fn=tail,
        _moment_fns={1: moment_1, 2: moment_2, ...},
    )


class MyProcess(Process):
    def __init__(self, param1: float, param2: float) -> None:
        # validate parameters
        # store self.param1, self.param2
        # build CompositionNode with math_note and reference
        super().__init__(exactness=ExactnessLevel.EXACT, _node=node)

    def _triplet(self) -> LevyTriplet:
        # Return LevyTriplet(b=..., sigma_sq=..., nu=...)
        # b must be consistent with the truncation h(x) = 1_{|x|≤1}
        # If b is computed by quadrature, use an exact formula (like E_1)
        # when available. See gamma.py for the pattern.

    def _properties(self) -> ProcessProperties:
        return ProcessProperties(
            has_stationary_increments=True,
            has_independent_increments=True,
            is_martingale=...,      # True only if drift=0 and ∫_{|x|>1} x ν(dx) = 0
            has_finite_variance=...,
            has_finite_mean=...,
            self_similarity_index=None,   # fill if self-similar
            tail_index=...,               # α such that ν((x,∞)) ~ x^{-α}, or None
            is_subordinator=...,          # True only if support ⊂ (0,∞)
        )

    def cumulants(self, order: int) -> dict[int, float]:
        # Override with exact closed-form formulas where known.
        # Fall back to super().cumulants() only if no formula exists.
        ...

    def char_func_exact(self, u, t=1.0) -> np.ndarray:
        # If the characteristic function has a closed form, implement it here
        # and override char_func() to call it.
        ...

    def char_func(self, u, t=1.0) -> np.ndarray:
        return self.char_func_exact(u=u, t=t)  # if closed form exists

    def simulate(self, n_steps, n_paths=1, T=1.0, rng=None) -> np.ndarray:
        # Use the most efficient exact algorithm known.
        # Return shape (n_paths, n_steps + 1), paths[:, 0] == 0.
        ...

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f"MyProcess(param1={self.param1}, param2={self.param2})"

2. Add to spxa/zoo/levy/__init__.py

from spxa.zoo.levy.<name> import MyProcess
# add to __all__

3. Add to spxa/zoo/__init__.py

from spxa.zoo.levy import ..., MyProcess
# add to __all__

4. Add to spxa/__init__.py

from spxa.zoo import ..., MyProcess
# add to __all__

5. Create tests/exactness/test_<name>.py

Every test must have @pytest.mark.exactness and cite the formula being verified. Minimum required tests:

@pytest.mark.exactness
def test_<name>_no_gaussian_component() -> None:
    """σ²=0 for pure-jump processes. <Primary reference>."""
    ...

@pytest.mark.exactness
def test_<name>_char_func_at_zero() -> None:
    """φ(0;t)=1. Definition of characteristic function."""
    ...

@pytest.mark.exactness
def test_<name>_char_func_time_additivity() -> None:
    """φ(u;s+t)=φ(u;s)·φ(u;t). Sato (1999), Definition 1.6."""
    ...

@pytest.mark.exactness
def test_<name>_cumulant_1() -> None:
    """κ₁ = <formula>. <Reference, equation number>."""
    ...

@pytest.mark.exactness
def test_<name>_cumulant_2() -> None:
    """κ₂ = <formula>. <Reference, equation number>."""
    ...

@pytest.mark.exactness
def test_<name>_simulate_mean() -> None:
    """Empirical mean converges to κ₁. Law of large numbers."""
    ...

@pytest.mark.exactness
def test_<name>_simulate_variance() -> None:
    """Empirical variance converges to κ₂."""
    ...

If the process is a subordinator, also add:

@pytest.mark.exactness
def test_<name>_is_subordinator() -> None:
    """Paths are non-decreasing. <Reference>."""
    ...

@pytest.mark.exactness
def test_<name>_simulate_non_decreasing() -> None:
    """All increments non-negative."""
    ...

6. Add to PROCESS_REGISTRY.md

Add a row to the table with: class name, exactness level, available cumulants, simulation algorithm, primary reference.

Pattern to copy: spxa/zoo/levy/gamma.py and tests/exactness/test_gamma.py are the reference implementation.

docs.title: B. New beyond-Lévy process (zoo/beyond)
docs.text:
Beyond-Lévy processes (fBM, Hawkes, OU-Lévy) violate stationarity or independence of increments and therefore have no Lévy–Khintchine triplet.

Files to create or modify:

1. Create spxa/zoo/beyond/<name>.py

Key differences from a Lévy process:

class MyBeyondProcess(Process):
    def __init__(self, ...) -> None:
        # ExactnessLevel is MOMENT_PROPAGATION, not EXACT
        super().__init__(exactness=ExactnessLevel.MOMENT_PROPAGATION, _node=node)

    def _triplet(self) -> LevyTriplet:
        # MUST raise ExactnessError with a clear explanation of
        # which Lévy property is violated and why no triplet exists.
        raise ExactnessError(
            method="triplet",
            required="EXACT",
            actual="MOMENT_PROPAGATION",
            reason="<process name> violates <stationary/independent> increments "
                   "because <mathematical reason>. No Lévy–Khintchine triplet exists. "
                   "Use <what to use instead>.",
        )

    def _properties(self) -> ProcessProperties:
        return ProcessProperties(
            has_stationary_increments=...,   # likely False or process-specific
            has_independent_increments=...,  # likely False
            ...
            notes=[
                "Human-readable explanation of why this is beyond Lévy.",
                "What analytical quantities ARE available.",
            ],
        )

    def _moment_propagation_cumulants(self, order: int) -> dict[int, float]:
        # Implement what you CAN compute: typically κ₁ and κ₂ exactly,
        # and float('nan') for higher orders that are intractable.
        result = {}
        if order >= 1:
            result[1] = ...
        if order >= 2:
            result[2] = ...
        for n in range(3, order + 1):
            result[n] = float('nan')
        return result

    # Add domain-specific analytical methods beyond what Process provides:
    def variance(self, t: float) -> float: ...
    def covariance(self, s: float, t: float) -> float: ...
    def autocovariance(self, h: float) -> float: ...

2. Add to spxa/zoo/beyond/__init__.py, spxa/zoo/__init__.py, spxa/__init__.py

Same pattern as Lévy processes.

3. Create tests/exactness/test_beyond.py entries

Add a class TestMyBeyondProcess to the existing tests/exactness/test_beyond.py. Required tests:

  • test_<name>_triplet_raises — verifies ExactnessError is raised
  • test_<name>_<analytical_property> — verifies each formula you implement against its cited source
  • test_<name>_simulate_* — verifies simulation statistics

Pattern to copy: spxa/zoo/beyond/fbm.py (fBM) and the TestFractionalBrownianMotion class in tests/exactness/test_beyond.py.

docs.title: C. New operation (ops/)
docs.text:
Operations are functions that take Process objects and return a new Process, or take a LevyTriplet and return a new LevyTriplet.

Before implementing, open an issue stating: - The mathematical definition of the operation - Whether the result is exact for independent Lévy processes, or approximate - The theorem or cited result justifying the computation - The ExactnessLevel propagation rule

Files to create or modify:

1. Create spxa/ops/<operation>.py

"""
<Operation name>.

Mathematical basis
------------------
State the theorem. Cite author, year, theorem number.

Exact for: <conditions under which result is EXACT>
Approximate for: <conditions under which it degrades and why>
"""

def <operation>(X: Process, Y: Process, ...) -> Process:
    """
    Brief description.

    Parameters / Returns / Raises / References sections.
    """
    ...

Rules: - If the operation is exact for independent Lévy processes, include a proof sketch or theorem citation in the docstring - If the result degrades ExactnessLevel, emit SpxaDegradationWarning with a mathematical reason — never silently degrade - If the operation requires conditions (e.g. Y must be a subordinator), check them explicitly and raise ValueError with a helpful message

2. Add to spxa/ops/__init__.py

Add the function/class to the imports and __all__.

3. Add tests to tests/unit/test_ops.py

Add a new test class. At minimum:

  • Correctness tests: verify the output against known exact values
  • Exactness tests: verify ExactnessLevel is set correctly
  • Error tests: verify that invalid inputs raise the right exceptions
  • Warning tests: verify that degradation emits SpxaDegradationWarning

If the operation touches the triplet, add a test that verifies the triplet arithmetic against Sato (1999) directly.

Pattern to copy: spxa/ops/subordination.py and the TestSubordination class in tests/unit/test_ops.py.

docs.title: D. New analytic tool (analytics/)
docs.text:
Analytic tools compute quantities derived from the characteristic function or cumulants of a process.

Files to create or modify:

1. Add to an existing spxa/analytics/<module>.py or create a new one

Every function must: - State clearly whether the result is exact or approximate - Say which processes it works for (EXACT only? MOMENT_PROPAGATION too?) - Raise ExactnessError if called on a process whose exactness level is insufficient - Cite the mathematical result being implemented

def my_analytic_function(
    process: Process,
    ...,
) -> float:
    """
    Brief description.

    Exact for EXACT processes via <formula>.
    Requires: <conditions>.

    Parameters
    ----------
    ...

    References
    ----------
    Author (year), equation/theorem number.
    """
    if process.exactness == ExactnessLevel.SIMULATION_ONLY:
        raise ExactnessError(...)
    ...

2. Add to spxa/analytics/__init__.py

3. Add tests to tests/unit/test_ops.py or a new tests/unit/test_analytics.py

At minimum: a test against a known value, a test for the correct error when called on an unsupported process.

Pattern to copy: spxa/analytics/divergence.py and the TestAnalyticsPipeline class in tests/integration/test_composition.py.

docs.title: E. New simulation algorithm (sim/)
docs.text:
Simulation functions produce sample paths or random variates. The bar is high: if you claim a sampler is "exact", it must be exact in distribution — not an approximation.

Files to create or modify:

1. Add to an existing spxa/sim/<module>.py or create a new one

def sample_<name>(
    param1: float,
    param2: float,
    dt: float,
    n_steps: int,
    n_paths: int,
    rng: np.random.Generator,
) -> np.ndarray:
    """
    Exact increments of <process name> via <algorithm name>.

    Algorithm (<primary citation>):
      1. ...
      2. ...

    Parameters
    ----------
    ...

    Returns
    -------
    np.ndarray
        Increments, shape (n_paths, n_steps). Call increments_to_paths()
        to prepend x0 and convert to paths.

    References
    ----------
    <Full citation, year, algorithm number if applicable>
    """
    ...

Conventions: - Standalone samplers return increments of shape (n_paths, n_steps), not paths. Use increments_to_paths() from sim/exact.py to convert. - If the algorithm is approximate (e.g. Euler-Maruyama approximation to an SDE), state the strong convergence order and conditions in the docstring. - If the algorithm is exact, cite the theorem guaranteeing this.

2. Add to spxa/sim/__init__.py

3. Add tests to tests/unit/test_sim.py

Required: - Shape test: assert increments.shape == (n_paths, n_steps) - Mean test: empirical mean vs theoretical mean (use pytest.approx) - Variance test: empirical variance vs theoretical variance - If the process is a subordinator: non-negativity test, monotonicity test

Statistical tests must use n_paths ≥ 5000 and loose tolerances (rel=0.05 or abs=0.1) — they are Monte Carlo, not exactness tests.

Pattern to copy: spxa/sim/exact.py (sample_gamma, sample_vg) and tests/unit/test_sim.py (TestExactSamplers).

docs.title: F. New multivariate process (zoo/multivariate)
docs.text:
Multivariate processes live in spxa/zoo/multivariate.py and use MultivariateLevyTriplet (matrix \(\Sigma\)) rather than LevyTriplet (scalar \(\sigma^2\)).

Files to create or modify:

1. Add to spxa/zoo/multivariate.py

class MyMultivariateProcess(Process):
    def __init__(self, dim: int, ...) -> None:
        self.dim = dim
        ...
        super().__init__(exactness=ExactnessLevel.EXACT, _node=node)

    def _triplet(self) -> LevyTriplet:
        # Return a 1-d projection triplet (e.g. trace of Σ as σ²)
        # for compatibility with the base class.
        ...

    def multivariate_triplet(self) -> MultivariateLevyTriplet:
        # Return the full d-dimensional triplet.
        ...

    def simulate(self, n_steps, n_paths=1, T=1.0, rng=None) -> np.ndarray:
        # Return shape (n_paths, n_steps + 1, dim).
        # paths[:, 0, :] == 0.
        ...

2. Add to spxa/zoo/__init__.py

3. Add tests to tests/unit/test_multivariate.py

Required: - Shape test: assert paths.shape == (n_paths, n_steps + 1, dim) - Starts at zero: np.testing.assert_array_equal(paths[:, 0, :], 0.0) - Covariance recovery: for a BM-based process, empirical covariance should match the theoretical \(\Sigma\) (use np.testing.assert_allclose(..., atol=0.1))

Pattern to copy: MultivariateBrownianMotion in multivariate.py and TestMultivariateBrownianMotion in tests/unit/test_multivariate.py.

docs.title: G. Core change (core/)
docs.text:
core/ is the algebraic foundation. Any change requires:

  1. Open an RFC issue using the RFC template in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/rfc.md. The RFC must state: motivation, proposed change, backward compatibility impact, and alternatives considered.
  2. Two maintainer approvals before implementation begins.
  3. Full backward compatibility or a deprecation plan spanning two minor versions (see Versioning).

Files in core/ and what they own:

  • exactness.py — the ExactnessLevel enum and combine(). Only add a new level if it is mathematically distinct from the three existing ones.
  • exceptions.py — SpxaError, ExactnessError, SpxaDegradationWarning. New exception subclasses must have a specific mathematical reason.
  • levy_measure.py — LevyMeasure hierarchy. New subclasses must implement density(), total_mass(), tail(), and moment().
  • process.py — Process base class and operators. The operator signatures (__add__, __mul__, __matmul__) are frozen after 1.0.0.
  • properties.py — ProcessProperties and propagation rules. Adding a new property requires updating all three combine_* static methods and all existing processes that set that property.
  • triplet.py — LevyTriplet. The b, sigma_sq, nu fields and the __add__, scale(), char_exp(), cumulant() methods are frozen after 1.0.0.

Test requirements for core changes:

  • All existing tests must still pass
  • New behavior must be covered by tests in tests/unit/test_core.py
  • If the change affects exactness propagation, add a test that verifies the exact ExactnessLevel of a composed process after the change

docs.title: H. Bug fix
docs.text:
Open a bug report issue first using the bug report template. If the bug is an exactness violation (spxa returned an analytically wrong value), add the label exactness-violation — this is the highest priority category.

Files to modify:

  1. Fix the bug in the relevant source file
  2. Add a test in the appropriate test file that would have caught the bug. For exactness violations, the test goes in tests/exactness/.
  3. Add an entry to CHANGELOG.md under ## Unreleased → ### Fixed

For exactness violations specifically:

The new test must cite the published formula that contradicts the wrong value spxa was returning. This test must go in tests/exactness/ and carry @pytest.mark.exactness. The fix must be verified against the published formula in the test, not just against the "fixed" code.

docs.title: I. Documentation
docs.text:
Theory docs (docs/theory/) are formal mathematical write-ups. They must be self-contained, cite primary sources, and match the code exactly — every formula in a theory doc must be implemented in the code and verified by an exactness test.

Tutorials (docs/tutorials/) are Jupyter notebooks. They must be runnable (jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute) and committed with outputs cleared.

API docs are auto-generated from docstrings via mkdocstrings. Improve API docs by improving the docstring in the source file, not by editing generated files.

Docstring format: NumPy style throughout. Every public function and class must have: a one-line summary, a Parameters section, a Returns section, and a References section citing the primary source. Equation numbers in citations are required for any non-obvious formula.

docs.title: The exactness test suite
docs.text:
tests/exactness/ is sacred. It is the mechanism by which spxa guarantees it never silently returns a wrong mathematical result.

Invariants that must never be violated:

  1. No test in tests/exactness/ may carry @pytest.mark.skip, @pytest.mark.skipif, or @pytest.mark.xfail for any reason. If a formula is wrong, fix the formula. If a test is wrong, fix the test. The scripts/check_exactness_markers.py script enforces this in CI.

  2. Every test must have @pytest.mark.exactness.

  3. Every test docstring must cite the exact theorem, equation, or section being verified. The citation must include author, year, and location (equation number, theorem number, or page). Example: 

    """κ₂(X₁) = σ² + θ²ν for VG. Madan, Carr & Chang (1998), Section 2."""

  4. The test must verify a closed-form result, not just "it runs without error" or "the output is positive". Compare against the mathematical formula, not against what the code produces.

  5. Statistical tests (empirical mean/variance) belong in tests/exactness/ only when verifying that the simulation converges to a theoretically known value. Use n_paths ≥ 10000 and tolerances abs=0.05 or rel=0.05 — small enough to catch real bugs, loose enough that they don't flake.

docs.title: Code style
docs.text:
Linting: ruff for linting and formatting — enforced by pre-commit and CI. Configuration in pyproject.toml.

Type checking: mypy in strict mode — enforced by CI.

Naming: - Process classes: PascalCase (e.g. VarianceGamma, NIG) - Functions: snake_case - Private helpers: _snake_case - Lévy measure constructors: _<processname>_levy_measure()

No comment line breaks. Lines like # ==== or # ---- are prohibited. Section structure comes from function/class definitions.

No commented-out code in PRs. Use git history.

No unnecessary comments. A comment that restates what the code obviously does is noise. Comments should explain why, especially for non-obvious mathematical choices.

Docstrings are not optional. Every public function, class, and method must have a NumPy-style docstring with a References section.

docs.title: Commit conventions
docs.text:
Use conventional commits:

feat(zoo): add TemperedStable — exact cumulants, rejection simulation
feat(ops): add exponential() — stochastic exponential of a semimartingale
fix(zoo/vg): eliminate singularity warning in triplet drift
test(exactness): VG — char_func vs time-additivity
docs(theory): add derivation of subordination triplet formula
chore: update PROCESS_REGISTRY with TemperedStable entry

Scope is the module: core, zoo, zoo/levy, zoo/beyond, ops, analytics, sim, story, docs, test, chore.

Commit granularity: commit after each logical unit of work. Do not batch unrelated changes. Do not commit broken states.

After each commit that adds a feature or fix, push to the remote. The CI runs on every push and a failing CI is a blocking issue.

docs.title: Versioning and deprecation
docs.text:
spxa follows semantic versioning strictly.

core/ and ops/ APIs are frozen after 1.0.0. Adding parameters with defaults is allowed. Removing parameters, changing return types, or changing operator semantics requires a major version bump.

Deprecations must: 1. Emit DeprecationWarning with a clear message stating what to use instead 2. Remain in the codebase for at least two minor versions before removal 3. Have an entry in CHANGELOG.md under ### Deprecated

Breaking changes require: 1. A major version bump 2. An entry in CHANGELOG.md under ### Removed 3. A migration note in the changelog explaining what to do

Every PR must add an entry to CHANGELOG.md under ## Unreleased in the appropriate section (Added, Changed, Fixed, Deprecated, Removed).

docs.title: Differentiable SDE Engine & Hardware Acceleration (spxa.diff)
docs.text: The spxa.diff subpackage provides JAX-accelerated, hardware-vectorized, and end-to-end differentiable simulation and sensitivity engines for continuous and jump-diffusion stochastic differential equations (SDEs).

docs.title: Key Capabilities
docs.text:
1. JIT Compilation & Hardware Acceleration:
  2. Compiles full simulation trajectories to native GPU/TPU/CPU machine instructions via jax.lax.scan and jax.jit.

  3. Vectorized batch parallel simulation across hundreds of thousands of Monte Carlo paths via jax.vmap.

  4. Differentiable Numerical SDE Solvers:

  5. solve_euler_maruyama: Standard Itô and Jump-Diffusion discretization.
  6. solve_milstein: Order 1.0 strong convergence with automatic spatial diffusion derivatives computed via forward-mode autodiff (jax.jvp).
  7. solve_srk: Two-stage explicit Stochastic Runge-Kutta predictor-corrector.

  8. solve_reversible_heun: Reversible trapezoidal integrator for memory-efficient backpropagation through time.

  9. Differentiable Stochastic Processes:

  10. Diffusions: DifferentiableGBM, DifferentiableOU, DifferentiableCIR, DifferentiableBESQ, DifferentiableBessel, DifferentiableCEV, DifferentiableBilinear.
  11. Stochastic Volatility: DifferentiableHeston, DifferentiableSABR, DifferentiableThreeHalves.
  12. Jump Diffusions: DifferentiableMerton, DifferentiableKou, DifferentiableBates, DifferentiableHawkes.
  13. Multi-Factor & Commodities: DifferentiableSchwartz1Factor, DifferentiableSchwartz2Factor, DifferentiableVectorOU.

  14. Fractional & Rough: simulate_diff_fbm, simulate_diff_rough_heston.

  15. Sensitivity & Greek Differentiation Engine (spxa.diff.greeks):

  16. Pathwise Automatic Differentiation: \(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathbb{E}[f(X_T)]\).
  17. Likelihood Ratio Method (LRM): Score function sensitivities for discontinuous payoffs (e.g. digital options, barrier options).
  18. Malliavin Greeks: Integration-by-parts on Wiener space via Bismut-Elworthy-Li weights for nonsmooth payoffs.

  19. Higher-Order Hessian Greeks: Second-order cross-Greeks (\(\Gamma, \text{Vanna}, \text{Volga}\)) via jax.hessian.

  20. Neural SDEs & Deep Hedging (spxa.diff.nn):

  21. DifferentiableNeuralSDE: Parameterized drift and diffusion networks.
  22. Deep Hedging Engine: Multi-period optimal hedging under transaction costs and convex risk measures (Entropic risk, Expected Shortfall, Quadratic error).

docs.title: Portfolio AAD & Universal Risk Engine (spxa.risk)
docs.text: The spxa.risk module delivers Tier-1 institutional risk analytics, real-time XVA modeling, regulatory margin and capital engines (ISDA-SIMM and FRTB), and automated Adjoint Algorithmic Differentiation (AAD) across complex multi-asset derivative portfolios.

docs.title: 1. Financial Instruments & Bilateral Portfolios (spxa.risk.instruments, spxa.risk.portfolio)
docs.text:
• Derivatives: EuropeanOption, BarrierOption (discrete/continuous monitoring with in-out parity), AsianOption (running arithmetic average), BasketOption, InterestRateSwap (IRS), and CreditDefaultSwap (CDS).
  • Netting Sets & CSA: Bilateral netting agreements governing independent amounts, uncollateralized thresholds (\(H_C\)), Minimum Transfer Amounts (MTA), and Margin Periods of Risk (MPOR).
  • Dynamic Exposure Profiles: Time-dependent Expected Exposure (\(\text{EE}(t)\)), Potential Future Exposure (\(\text{PFE}_{95}(t)\), \(\text{PFE}_{99}(t)\)), and Expected Positive Exposure (\(\text{EPE}\)).

docs.title: 2. Portfolio Adjoint Algorithmic Differentiation (AAD) (spxa.risk.aad)
docs.text:
Computes the full portfolio Present Value, Delta vector, Vega matrix, and second-order Cross-Gamma Hessian matrix in a single reverse-mode backward pass: $\( oldsymbol{\Delta} = abla_{ oldsymbol{S}_0} \Pi_0, \quad oldsymbol{\mathcal{V}} = abla_{ oldsymbol{\sigma}} \Pi_0, \quad oldsymbol{\Gamma} = abla^2_{ oldsymbol{S}_0} \Pi_0\)$

Includes smooth mollifiers (smooth_indicator) for robust differentiation through non-smooth barrier and digital contract boundaries.

docs.title: 3. Real-Time XVA Engine (spxa.risk.xva)
docs.text: Evaluates comprehensive bilateral valuation adjustments: $\(\text{Total XVA} = \text{CVA} - \text{DVA} + \text{FVA} + \text{MVA} + \text{KVA}\)$ - Credit Valuation Adjustment (CVA): Counterparty default risk under collateralization. - Debit Valuation Adjustment (DVA): Own-default risk and credit benefit. - Funding Valuation Adjustment (FVA): Funding Cost Adjustment (FCA) and Funding Benefit Adjustment (FBA) over uncollateralized exposure. - Margin Valuation Adjustment (MVA): Funding cost of dynamic initial margin posting over the trade lifecycle. - Capital Valuation Adjustment (KVA): Hurdle cost of holding economic and regulatory capital.

docs.title: 4. Regulatory Margin & Capital (spxa.risk.frtb_simm)
docs.text:
• ISDA SIMM v2.6+ Engine: Multi-class margin aggregation (Equity, Interest Rate, Credit, Commodity, FX) incorporating intra-bucket and cross-class correlation matrices.
  • FRTB Standardized Approach (SA): Sensitivities-Based Method (SBM) capital requirements across Low, Medium, and High correlation scenarios with Default Risk Charges (DRC).

docs.title: 5. Universal Scenario Generator & Stress Testing (spxa.risk.scenarios, spxa.risk.reporting)
docs.text:
• Historical crisis replay (LEHMAN_2008, COVID_MARCH_2020, INFLATION_SHOCK_2022).
  • Reverse stress testing identifying minimal market displacements that breach loss thresholds.
  • Executive risk reporting (format_risk_executive_summary).

docs.title: Beyond the Lévy Regime
docs.text: spxa is built on Lévy process arithmetic, but many processes used in practice fall outside the Lévy class. This document explains how spxa handles them, what guarantees are maintained, and what is lost.

docs.title: Why the Lévy boundary matters
docs.text:
The Lévy–Khintchine triplet is defined only for processes with stationary and independent increments. Many important processes violate one or both:

Process Stationary increments Independent increments Lévy? Brownian motion yes yes yes Poisson process yes yes yes Variance Gamma yes yes yes Fractional BM (\(H \neq 1/2\)) yes no no Hawkes process no no no OU-Lévy no no no Brownian bridge no yes no

The loss of independent increments means the Lévy–Khintchine formula no longer applies. No triplet exists. Arithmetic cannot be exact.

docs.title: Fractional Brownian motion
docs.text:
Definition (Mandelbrot & Van Ness 1968). The fractional Brownian motion (fBM) \(B^H = (B^H_t)_{t \geq 0}\) with Hurst index \(H \in (0, 1)\) is the unique (up to scaling) centered Gaussian process with covariance

\[\mathbb{E}[B^H_s B^H_t] = \frac{1}{2}\left(|s|^{2H} + |t|^{2H} - |s-t|^{2H}\right)\]

For \(H = 1/2\), fBM is standard Brownian motion. For \(H \neq 1/2\), fBM has long memory (for \(H > 1/2\)) or anti-persistence (for \(H < 1/2\)), and its increments are correlated. It is not a semimartingale for \(H \neq 1/2\), which means Itô calculus does not apply and the Lévy–Khintchine representation does not exist.

What spxa tracks for fBM:

  • The Hurst index \(H\) as the fundamental parameter
  • Self-similarity: \(B^H_{ct} \stackrel{d}{=} c^H B^H_t\), so \(H\) propagates under scaling as \(c \cdot B^H \sim c^1\) in scale, Hurst index preserved
  • Variance: \(\text{Var}(B^H_t) = t^{2H}\)
  • The Hölder regularity: paths are \((H - \varepsilon)\)-Hölder continuous for every \(\varepsilon > 0\)

What spxa does not and cannot track exactly:

  • A distributional triplet (does not exist)
  • Cumulants of compositions involving fBM (only approximated via moment propagation)
  • Addition of fBM with a Lévy process: the result is not fBM and not a Lévy process; spxa degrades to MOMENT_PROPAGATION and issues a warning

spxa's Hurst algebra. For compositions of fBM processes:

  • \(c \cdot B^H\): Hurst index preserved, variance scaled by \(c^2\)
  • \(B^{H_1} + B^{H_2}\) (independent): mean and variance propagate; Hurst index of the sum is \(\max(H_1, H_2)\) asymptotically (the dominant long-memory component governs long-run autocorrelation), but this is an approximation and is flagged as such

docs.title: Hawkes processes
docs.text:
Definition (Hawkes 1971). A Hawkes process \(N = (N_t)_{t \geq 0}\) is a point process with conditional intensity

\[\lambda(t) = \mu + \int_0^t h(t - s)\, dN_s\]

where \(\mu > 0\) is the background rate and \(h : [0, \infty) \to [0, \infty)\) is the excitation kernel satisfying \(\int_0^\infty h(s)\, ds < 1\) (subcriticality condition). The process is self-exciting: each event increases the probability of future events.

A Hawkes process does not have stationary increments (conditional on the history, increments are non-stationary) and is not a Lévy process.

What spxa tracks for Hawkes processes:

  • The mean intensity: \(\bar{\lambda} = \mu / (1 - \|h\|_1)\) where \(\|h\|_1 = \int_0^\infty h(s)\, ds\)
  • The variance of \(N_t\): \(\text{Var}(N_t) \approx \bar{\lambda} t \cdot (1 - \|h\|_1)^{-1}\) for large \(t\) (asymptotic result, Hawkes & Oakes 1974)
  • The Fano factor: \(F = \text{Var}(N_t) / \mathbb{E}[N_t]\), which is always \(\geq 1\), measuring burstiness
  • Stationarity of the intensity in the stationary regime (when \(t \to \infty\))

spxa's exactness for Hawkes: MOMENT_PROPAGATION. Simulation uses Ogata's thinning algorithm.

docs.title: OU-Lévy processes
docs.text:
Definition (Barndorff-Nielsen & Shephard 2001). The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process driven by a Lévy subordinator \(L\) is defined by the SDE

\[dV_t = -\lambda V_t\, dt + dL_{\lambda t}\]

with \(\lambda > 0\) and \(L\) a subordinator (non-decreasing Lévy process). The solution is

\[V_t = e^{-\lambda t} V_0 + \int_0^t e^{-\lambda(t-s)}\, dL_{\lambda s}\]

Unlike a Lévy process, \(V\) does not have independent increments (the decay structure creates serial dependence). However, it does have a stationary distribution which is infinitely divisible, with a known Lévy–Khintchine triplet. The stationary distribution of \(V\) has Lévy measure \(\nu_V(dx) = \int_x^\infty \nu_L(dy)/y\) (Barndorff-Nielsen & Shephard 2001, Proposition 2.1).

What spxa tracks for OU-Lévy:

  • The stationary distribution exactly (triplet is known)
  • The autocovariance: \(\text{Cov}(V_t, V_{t+h}) = e^{-\lambda h} \text{Var}(V_\infty)\)
  • The mean reversion rate \(\lambda\)
  • The marginal moments exactly from the stationary distribution's triplet

spxa's exactness for OU-Lévy: MOMENT_PROPAGATION for path-level operations; the stationary distribution is EXACT.

docs.title: Degradation policy
docs.text:
When an operation mixes process types or leaves the Lévy regime, spxa:

  1. Sets ExactnessLevel to the lowest level among operands
  2. Issues a SpxaDegradationWarning with a message stating: which operation caused the degradation, what mathematical property was lost, and what is still being tracked exactly
  3. Raises ExactnessError if a method requiring a higher exactness level is called on the result (e.g., calling .triplet on a fBM + Gamma sum)

This design ensures the library never silently returns a wrong answer by pretending an approximate result is exact.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Mandelbrot, B. B. & Van Ness, J. W. (1968). Fractional Brownian motions, fractional noises and applications. SIAM Review, 10(4), 422–437.
  • Hawkes, A. G. (1971). Spectra of some self-exciting and mutually exciting point processes. Biometrika, 58(1), 83–90.
  • Hawkes, A. G. & Oakes, D. (1974). A cluster process representation of a self-exciting process. Journal of Applied Probability, 11(3), 493–503.
  • Barndorff-Nielsen, O. E. & Shephard, N. (2001). Non-Gaussian Ornstein–Uhlenbeck-based models and some of their uses in financial economics. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B, 63(2), 167–241.
  • Applebaum, D. (2009). Lévy Processes and Stochastic Calculus, 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press. Chapter 4.

docs.title: Estimation and Calibration
docs.text:
There are two separate problems here. Estimation fits a model to the historical path of an observed (or partly observed) time series. Calibration fits a pricing model to today's cross-section of option quotes. spxa.calibration covers both. It has exact-likelihood estimators, moment and characteristic-function methods, nonlinear filters for latent states, smile and surface calibrators, and diagnostics that report uncertainty and goodness of fit.

docs.title: 1. Maximum likelihood from transition densities
docs.text:
Let \(X_0, X_\Delta, \dots, X_{N\Delta}\) be observed on a regular grid. For a Markov diffusion the likelihood factorises into transition densities:

\[ \ell(\theta) = \sum_{k=1}^{N} \log p_\theta\big(X_{k\Delta} \mid X_{(k-1)\Delta}\big). \]

Whenever \(p_\theta\) is known in closed form, the estimators in spxa.calibration.mle use it. They do not use an Euler (Gaussian) approximation, so the MLE has no discretisation bias at any sampling frequency. Without a closed-form density one would need approximations such as the Aït-Sahalia (2002) expansion, which spxa does not currently implement.

Model Dynamics Exact transition Brownian motion \(dX = \mu\,dt + \sigma\,dW\) \(\mathcal N(X + \mu\Delta,\ \sigma^2\Delta)\) GBM \(dS = \mu S\,dt + \sigma S\,dW\) \(\log S' \sim \mathcal N\big(\log S + (\mu-\tfrac12\sigma^2)\Delta,\ \sigma^2\Delta\big)\) OU / Vasicek \(dX = \kappa(\theta - X)\,dt + \sigma\,dW\) \(\mathcal N\big(X e^{-\kappa\Delta} + \theta(1-e^{-\kappa\Delta}),\ \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa}(1-e^{-2\kappa\Delta})\big)\) CIR \(dr = \kappa(\theta - r)\,dt + \sigma\sqrt r\,dW\) scaled non-central \(\chi^2\) (below) BESQ\(^\delta\) \(dX = \delta\,dt + 2\sqrt X\,dW\) \(X'/\Delta \sim \chi^2_\delta(X/\Delta)\)

CIR. Set \(c = 2\kappa / \big(\sigma^2(1 - e^{-\kappa\Delta})\big)\). Then \(2c\,r_{t+\Delta}\) given \(r_t\) is non-central \(\chi^2\) with \(4\kappa\theta/\sigma^2\) degrees of freedom and non-centrality \(2c\,r_t e^{-\kappa\Delta}\). Write \(u = c\,r_t e^{-\kappa\Delta}\), \(v = c\,r_{t+\Delta}\) and \(q = 2\kappa\theta/\sigma^2 - 1\). The density is

\[ p(r_{t+\Delta}\mid r_t) = c\, e^{-u-v}\Big(\frac{v}{u}\Big)^{q/2} I_q\big(2\sqrt{uv}\big). \]

CIRMaximumLikelihood evaluates \(I_q\) through the exponentially scaled Bessel function scipy.special.ive. This keeps \(\log I_q(z) = \log \mathrm{ive}_q(z) + z\) finite for large \(uv\). The log-likelihood matches scipy.stats.ncx2.logpdf (with Jacobian \(2c\)) to machine precision.

Heavy tails. StudentTInnovationsMLE fits location, scale and degrees of freedom \(\nu\) to i.i.d. returns. NormalInverseGaussianMLE fits the four-parameter NIG law, whose density involves \(K_1\). Both are i.i.d. return models. For a Lévy process observed at frequency \(\Delta\), the increment law is the \(\Delta\)-convolution power, which is the setting of §2.2.

Numerical optimisation

Every TimeSeriesEstimator maximises \(\ell\) with L-BFGS-B from default_initial_guess within default_bounds. It returns an EstimationResult with the parameters, standard errors, log-likelihood, AIC/BIC and the number of observations. These can be fed straight into §4.

docs.title: 2.1 GMM
docs.text:
Suppose a model implies \(\mathbb E[m(X_t;\theta_0)] = 0\) for an \(m\)-vector of moment functions, with \(m \ge k = \dim\theta\). Let \(g_N(\theta) = \frac1N\sum_t m(X_t;\theta)\). GMMEstimator implements two-step feasible GMM (Hansen 1982):

\[ \hat\theta = \arg\min_\theta\ g_N(\theta)^\top W\, g_N(\theta), \qquad W^{(1)} = I,\quad W^{(2)} = \hat\Omega^{-1}. \]

Here \(\hat\Omega\) estimates the long-run covariance \(\sum_{j\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{Cov}(m_t, m_{t-j})\) at the first-step estimate. With the efficient weight, \(\sqrt N(\hat\theta - \theta_0) \Rightarrow \mathcal N\big(0, (G^\top\Omega^{-1}G)^{-1}\big)\), where \(G = \mathbb E[\partial m/\partial\theta^\top]\).

OrnsteinUhlenbeckGMM uses the stationary mean, variance, lag-one autocovariance and third central moment:

\[ \mathbb E[X-\theta]=0,\quad \mathbb E[(X-\theta)^2]=\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa},\quad \mathbb E[(X_t-\theta)(X_{t-\Delta}-\theta)]=\tfrac{\sigma^2}{2\kappa}e^{-\kappa\Delta},\quad \mathbb E[(X-\theta)^3]=0. \]

CIRGMM uses the analogous conditions with stationary variance \(\sigma^2\theta/(2\kappa)\).

HAC covariance. newey_west_hac returns

\[ \hat\Omega = \hat\Gamma_0 + \sum_{j\ge1} k\!\Big(\frac{j}{L+1}\Big)\big(\hat\Gamma_j + \hat\Gamma_j^\top\big), \qquad \hat\Gamma_j = \frac1N\sum_t \tilde m_t \tilde m_{t-j}^\top, \]

where \(\tilde m\) is the demeaned moment series. The default lag is \(L = \lfloor 4(N/100)^{2/9}\rfloor\). Two kernels are available: Bartlett, \(k(x) = 1-x\) on \([0,1]\) (Newey & West 1987), and quadratic-spectral, \(k(x) = \frac{25}{12\pi^2x^2}\big(\frac{\sin(6\pi x/5)}{6\pi x/5} - \cos(6\pi x/5)\big)\) over all lags (Andrews 1991). The result is projected onto the positive semi-definite cone by eigenvalue clipping.

Over-identification. hansen_j_test computes \(J = N\,g_N(\hat\theta)^\top\hat\Omega^{-1}g_N(\hat\theta) \Rightarrow \chi^2_{m-k}\) under correct specification. With \(m = k\) the model is exactly identified and \(J\) is uninformative.

docs.title: 2.2 Empirical characteristic function
docs.text:
For Lévy and affine jump models the density is often unavailable, but the characteristic function \(\varphi_\theta(u) = \mathbb E[e^{iuX_\Delta}]\) is known through Lévy–Khintchine. ECFEstimator minimises

\[ \hat\theta = \arg\min_\theta \int \big|\hat\varphi_N(u) - \varphi_\theta(u)\big|^2 w(u)\,du, \qquad \hat\varphi_N(u) = \frac1N\sum_{j=1}^N e^{iuX_j}. \]

The integral is a quadrature on a grid, by default 41 points on \([-10,10]\). The weight is Gaussian, \(w(u)=e^{-u^2/2}\), or uniform. Any process in the zoo with a char_func can be plugged in. The estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal for i.i.d. increments (Feuerverger & McDunnough 1981; Yu 2004). Its efficiency depends on the grid and the weight.

docs.title: 3. Latent states: filtering and quasi-likelihood
docs.text:
Many models have unobserved state, such as stochastic variance, convenience yield or default intensity. Write the discrete state-space model

\[ x_k = f(x_{k-1}) + \eta_k,\ \ \eta_k\sim(0, Q(x_{k-1})), \qquad y_k = h(x_k) + \varepsilon_k,\ \ \varepsilon_k\sim\mathcal N(0, R). \]

Every filter returns a FilteredTrajectory with the filtered means and covariances, the innovations and a log-likelihood.

docs.title: 3.1 Unscented Kalman filter
docs.text:
UnscentedKalmanFilter uses the scaled sigma-point set of van der Merwe. For state dimension \(L\), \(\lambda = \alpha^2(L+\kappa) - L\), and the \(2L+1\) points are

\[ \mathcal X_0 = \bar x,\qquad \mathcal X_{\pm i} = \bar x \pm \big(\sqrt{(L+\lambda)P}\big)_i, \]

with weights

\[ W^{m}_0 = \tfrac{\lambda}{L+\lambda},\quad W^{c}_0 = W^m_0 + 1 - \alpha^2 + \beta,\quad W^{m}_i = W^{c}_i = \tfrac{1}{2(L+\lambda)}. \]

The defaults are \(\alpha = 10^{-3}\), \(\beta = 2\) and \(\kappa = 0\). Propagating the points through \(f\) and \(h\) gives the predicted mean and covariance, \(P_{yy}\) and \(P_{xy}\). These are correct to second order for any smooth nonlinearity, and exact when \(f\) and \(h\) are affine, in which case the UKF is the Kalman filter. The log-likelihood is the prediction-error decomposition

\[ \ell = -\tfrac12\sum_k\Big(\log\det(2\pi S_k) + v_k^\top S_k^{-1}v_k\Big), \qquad v_k = y_k - \hat y_{k|k-1},\ S_k = P_{yy,k}. \]

QuasiMaximumLikelihoodEstimator maximises this \(\ell\) over the model parameters. When the model is not linear-Gaussian this is a quasi-likelihood. The estimator is still consistent under standard conditions, but standard errors should use the sandwich form of §4.

docs.title: 3.2 Bootstrap particle filter
docs.text:
BootstrapParticleFilter implements sequential importance resampling (Gordon, Salmond & Smith 1993) with \(N\) particles (500 by default). Each step does the following:

  1. Propagate \(x_k^{(i)} \sim p(x_k\mid x_{k-1}^{(i)})\).
  2. Update the weights, \(w_k^{(i)} \propto w_{k-1}^{(i)}\,p(y_k\mid x_k^{(i)})\), in log-space.
  3. Accumulate \(\log\hat p(y_k\mid y_{1:k-1}) = \log\sum_i w_{k-1}^{(i)}p(y_k\mid x_k^{(i)})\).
  4. Resample systematically if \(\mathrm{ESS} = 1/\sum_i (w_k^{(i)})^2 < 0.5N\), then reset the weights to \(1/N\).

The product of the incremental terms is an unbiased estimator of the likelihood (Del Moral 2004). This is what particle-marginal Metropolis–Hastings requires. Its logarithm is biased downwards by about half its variance. systematic_resample, stratified_resample and effective_sample_size are exported separately.

Optimising a particle likelihood

\(\hat\ell(\theta)\) is a random, non-smooth function of \(\theta\). To maximise it, fix the random seed (common random numbers) and prefer derivative-free optimisers.

docs.title: 3.3 Model-specific filters
docs.text:
Filter State Observation HestonVarianceFilter \(x = \log v\), with Euler drift \(\big(\kappa(\theta-v) - \tfrac12\sigma^2\big)/v\) and variance \(\approx\sigma^2\Delta/v\) (Itô on \(\log v\)) volatility proxy \(y\approx\sqrt v = e^{x/2}\) SchwartzTwoFactorFilter \((\log S, \delta)\) with \(d\log S = (r-\delta-\tfrac12\sigma_1^2)dt + \sigma_1dW_1\) and \(d\delta = \kappa(\alpha-\delta)dt + \sigma_2dW_2\) log-futures, affine in the state through \(B(\tau) = (1-e^{-\kappa\tau})/\kappa\) DefaultIntensityFilter CIR intensity \(\lambda\) (Duffie–Singleton) CDS spread \(\approx \mathrm{LGD}\cdot\big(\theta + (\lambda-\theta)\frac{1-e^{-\kappa T}}{\kappa T}\big)\)

Working in \(\log v\) keeps the variance filter positive. The Schwartz measurement equation is affine, so its UKF is the exact Kalman filter for the Euler-discretised state.

docs.title: 4. Inference, standard errors and model selection
4.1 Information matrices
docs.text:
Let \(\hat\theta\) maximise \(\ell(\theta) = \sum_t \ell_t(\theta)\). Let \(H = \nabla^2\ell(\hat\theta)\) be the observed Hessian and \(s_t = \nabla\ell_t(\hat\theta)\) the per-observation scores.

fisher_information_matrix returns the observed information \(\mathcal I = -H\), using compute_numerical_hessian (central differences). Under correct specification, \(\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\theta) = \mathcal I^{-1}\).

sandwich_covariance_matrix returns the robust (Huber–White) estimator (White 1982):

\[ \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\theta) = H^{-1}\Big(\sum_t s_ts_t^\top\Big)H^{-1}. \]

This remains valid under misspecification, including QMLE (§3.1) and heavy-tailed returns fitted with a Gaussian likelihood. If the model is correct, the information-matrix equality makes the two estimators agree asymptotically.

Both use the Moore–Penrose pseudo-inverse. A near-singular \(H\) signals weak identification, and its standard errors should not be trusted. Information Geometry interprets \(\mathcal I\) as the Fisher–Rao metric.

docs.title: 4.2 Wald and profile-likelihood intervals
docs.text:
compute_parameter_inference turns a covariance matrix into standard errors \(\mathrm{se}_j = \sqrt{\hat V_{jj}}\), \(z\)-statistics \(\hat\theta_j/\mathrm{se}_j\), two-sided normal \(p\)-values and Wald intervals \(\hat\theta_j \pm z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\mathrm{se}_j\).

Wald intervals are symmetric by construction, so they can cross parameter bounds or misstate the uncertainty when \(\ell\) is skewed. This happens, for example, with a mean-reversion speed estimated from a short sample. compute_profile_likelihood instead evaluates

\[ \ell_p(\psi) = \max_{\lambda}\ \ell(\psi, \lambda) \]

on a grid of the target parameter \(\psi\), re-optimising the nuisance parameters \(\lambda\) at each point. It reports the likelihood-ratio interval

\[ \Big\{\psi : 2\big(\ell(\hat\theta) - \ell_p(\psi)\big) \le \chi^2_{1,1-\alpha}\Big\}, \]

which is invariant to reparametrisation and can be asymmetric.

docs.title: 4.3 Information criteria
docs.text:
With \(k\) parameters, \(n\) observations and maximised log-likelihood \(\hat\ell\):

Criterion Function Formula AIC akaike_information_criterion \(2k - 2\hat\ell\) AICc corrected_aic \(\mathrm{AIC} + \dfrac{2k(k+1)}{n-k-1}\) (infinite if \(n \le k+1\)) BIC bayesian_information_criterion \(k\log n - 2\hat\ell\) HQIC hannan_quinn_criterion \(2k\log\log n - 2\hat\ell\)

Smaller is better. AIC targets predictive Kullback–Leibler risk and is not consistent. BIC and HQIC are consistent for the true model when it is in the candidate set. ModelComparisonTable ranks fitted models by AIC and reports the differences \(\Delta_i\) and the Akaike weights \(e^{-\Delta_i/2}/\sum_j e^{-\Delta_j/2}\) (Burnham & Anderson 2002), with \(\Delta_i = \mathrm{AIC}_i - \min_j\mathrm{AIC}_j\).

Comparable likelihoods only

Information criteria compare likelihoods of the same data. Do not compare a model of prices with a model of log-returns, or an exact likelihood with a filter quasi-likelihood, without correcting for the transformation.

docs.title: 5. Smile and surface calibration
docs.text:
A MarketSurface holds the spot, rate, dividend yield and a list of MarketSlices of MarketQuotes (strike, maturity, quoted value and its quote_type, optional bid/ask, vega, forward and discount factor). A SurfaceCalibrator solves

\[ \hat\theta = \arg\min_{\theta\in\Theta}\ \mathcal L\big(\sigma^{\text{model}}(K_i,T_i;\theta),\ \sigma^{\text{mkt}}_i\big) + \text{penalty}(\theta). \]

docs.title: 5.1 Models
docs.text:
SABR. SABRCalibrator uses the Hagan et al. (2002) expansion for the Black implied vol. At the money it reduces to

\[ \sigma_{\text{ATM}} \approx \frac{\alpha}{F^{1-\beta}}\Big[1 + \Big(\frac{(1-\beta)^2\alpha^2}{24F^{2-2\beta}} + \frac{\rho\beta\nu\alpha}{4F^{1-\beta}} + \frac{2-3\rho^2}{24}\nu^2\Big)T\Big]. \]

\(\beta\) is usually fixed by convention (fixed_beta=1 for equity and FX, \(0.5\) for rates) because it is poorly identified jointly with \(\rho\). estimate_initial_alpha gives the leading-order start \(\alpha_0 = \sigma_{\text{ATM}}F^{1-\beta}\). The expansion is an asymptotic approximation and can imply a negative density far out of the money at long maturities.

Heston family. Calls are priced from the characteristic function of \(\log S_T\) through the Gil-Pelaez / Heston (1993) form

\[ C = S_0P_1 - Ke^{-rT}P_2,\qquad P_1 = \tfrac12 + \tfrac1\pi\int_0^\infty \operatorname{Re}\frac{e^{-iu\log K}\varphi(u-i)}{iu\,\varphi(-i)}du,\qquad P_2 = \tfrac12 + \tfrac1\pi\int_0^\infty \operatorname{Re}\frac{e^{-iu\log K}\varphi(u)}{iu}du, \]

where \(\varphi(-i) = \mathbb E[S_T] = S_0e^{rT}\). The integral uses Gauss–Legendre quadrature on \([0, 80]\). \(\varphi\) is evaluated in the Albrecher et al. (2007) "little trap" form, which avoids the complex-logarithm branch-cut discontinuity at long maturities. Model prices are then inverted to Black–Scholes implied vols by bounded root-finding.

Calibrator Parameters Characteristic function HestonCalibrator \(v_0,\kappa,\theta,\sigma,\rho\) Heston (1993) BatesCalibrator + \(\lambda, \mu_J, \sigma_J\) Heston × Merton log-normal jumps (Bates 1996) DoubleHestonCalibrator two independent variance factors product of two Heston factors (Christoffersen et al. 2009) CEVHestonCalibrator + CEV exponent \(\gamma\) (\(dS = rS\,dt + S^\gamma\sqrt v\,dW\)) heuristic: the Heston pricer with the local factor frozen at \(\sqrt{S_0K}\)

The CEV-Heston quote freezes \(S^{\gamma-1}\) at \(\sqrt{S_0K}\), i.e. it prices Heston with \(v_0\) and \(\theta\) multiplied by \((S_0K)^{\gamma-1}\). The vol-of-vol is not rescaled, so this is a fast heuristic rather than a convergent expansion. Validate it by Monte Carlo before relying on it away from \(\gamma = 1\).

The Heston, Bates and double-Heston pricers reduce to Black–Scholes as \(\sigma\to0\) with \(v_0=\theta\), and the Bates pricer reduces to the Merton (1976) series. Both limits are covered by exactness tests at non-zero rates. For other zoo processes, spxa.analytics.fourier.european_call_price gives Carr–Madan pricing from any char_func.

docs.title: 5.2 Loss functions
docs.text:
With errors \(e_i = \sigma^{\text{model}}_i - \sigma^{\text{mkt}}_i\):

Loss Residual RMSELoss \(e_i\), optionally \(\times\sqrt{w_i/\bar w}\) VegaWeightedLoss \(e_i\sqrt{\mathcal V_i/\bar{\mathcal V}}\), with vegas floored at min_vega RelativeErrorLoss \(e_i/\sigma^{\text{mkt}}_i\) ArbitragePenalizedLoss base loss plus penalties for violating the Feller condition \(2\kappa\theta\ge\sigma^2\) and for \(\lvert\rho\rvert\to1\), plus an optional user penalty

Vega weighting approximates a price-space fit, because \(\Delta C \approx \mathcal V\,\Delta\sigma\), while staying well scaled across strikes. The Feller penalty is a preference, not a no-arbitrage requirement. Equity-index Heston fits routinely violate it, and the CIR variance then touches zero but stays non-negative.

docs.title: 5.3 Optimisers
docs.text:
Box constraints are handled by ParameterTransform, the logit map \(u = \log\frac{x-a}{b-x}\) and its logistic inverse. This lets unconstrained optimisers work in \(\mathbb R^k\).

  • LeastSquaresOptimizer: bounded trust-region reflective least squares (scipy.optimize.least_squares, method trf). Fast but only local.
  • DifferentialEvolutionOptimizer: global and derivative-free. Robust to the flat valleys typical of Heston (\(\kappa\)–\(\theta\) and \(\sigma\)–\(\rho\) trade-offs).
  • HybridOptimizer: differential evolution followed by a TRF polish. This is the recommended default for stochastic-volatility models.

docs.title: 5.4 Fit diagnostics
docs.text:
analyze_surface_residuals reports RMSE, MAE, maximum error, mean relative error and per-tenor RMSE. It also counts static-arbitrage violations in the fitted surface:

  • calendar: total variance \(w = \sigma^2T\) must be non-decreasing in \(T\), checked at strikes common to adjacent maturities. This is exact for zero carry. With carry, the condition holds at fixed forward moneyness.
  • butterfly: call prices must be convex in strike.

docs.title: 6. Forecast diagnostics
docs.text:
A fitted model is a sequence of one-step-ahead predictive distributions \(F_t\). If the model is correct, the probability integral transforms \(u_t = F_t(y_t)\) are i.i.d. \(\mathcal U(0,1)\) (Rosenblatt 1952; Diebold, Gunther & Tay 1998). compute_pit_values computes \(u_t\), clipped to \([10^{-6}, 1-10^{-6}]\). evaluate_pit_diagnostics then runs two tests:

  • Kolmogorov–Smirnov test of uniformity.
  • Berkowitz (2001) likelihood-ratio test, described below.

For the Berkowitz test, map \(z_t = \Phi^{-1}(u_t)\) and fit the Gaussian AR(1) model \(z_t - \mu = \rho(z_{t-1}-\mu) + \sigma\varepsilon_t\). Then test \(H_0: \mu=0,\ \rho=0,\ \sigma^2=1\) with

\[ \mathrm{LR} = 2\big(\ell(\hat\mu,\hat\rho,\hat\sigma^2) - \ell(0,0,1)\big) \Rightarrow \chi^2_3. \]

Berkowitz has much more power than KS in small samples and also detects serial dependence, which KS cannot.

compute_residual_diagnostics applies Jarque–Bera (normality) and Ljung–Box (serial correlation, 10 lags by default) to standardised residuals or filter innovations. CalibrationReport collects parameters, standard errors, criteria and diagnostics into one summary, and plot_smile_overlay, plot_surface_error_heatmap and plot_filtered_trajectory visualise them.

docs.title: Copulas and Multivariate Dependence
docs.text:
A copula separates a joint distribution into its marginals and a dependence structure. This lets each asset keep its own process from the zoo while the coupling is modelled separately. spxa.copula provides elliptical, Archimedean and extreme-value families, exact concordance and tail-dependence measures, conditional sampling, rank-based estimation, and multi-asset simulation.

Object Implementation Abstract copula, Rosenblatt transforms, Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds spxa.copula.Copula Independence / comonotonic / countermonotonic IndependenceCopula, ComonotonicityCopula, CountermonotonicityCopula Elliptical GaussianCopula, StudentTCopula Archimedean ClaytonCopula, GumbelCopula, FrankCopula, JoeCopula, AliMikhailHaqCopula Extreme value GalambosCopula, HuslerReissCopula Estimation and selection pseudo_observations, fit_copula, select_best_copula Coupled multi-asset simulation and pricing CoupledProcess

docs.title: 1. Sklar's theorem
docs.text:
A \(d\)-dimensional copula is a distribution function on \([0,1]^d\) with uniform marginals. By Sklar's theorem (1959), every joint distribution \(H\) with marginals \(F_1,\dots,F_d\) can be written as

\[ H(x_1,\dots,x_d) = C\big(F_1(x_1),\dots,F_d(x_d)\big), \]

and \(C\) is unique on \(\operatorname{Ran}F_1\times\cdots\times\operatorname{Ran}F_d\). In particular \(C\) is unique when the marginals are continuous. Conversely, any copula combined with any marginals gives a valid joint law. With densities,

\[ h(x) = c\big(F_1(x_1),\dots,F_d(x_d)\big)\prod_{j=1}^d f_j(x_j), \qquad c = \frac{\partial^d C}{\partial u_1\cdots\partial u_d}. \]

Copulas are invariant under strictly increasing transformations of the coordinates. Rank statistics, such as Kendall's \(\tau\) and Spearman's \(\rho_S\), are functions of \(C\) alone. Every copula lies between the Fréchet–Hoeffding bounds (Copula.frechet_hoeffding_bounds):

\[ W(u) = \max\Big(\textstyle\sum_j u_j - d + 1,\ 0\Big) \;\le\; C(u) \;\le\; M(u) = \min_j u_j . \]

\(M\) is the comonotonic copula. \(W\) is a copula only for \(d=2\), where it is the countermonotonic copula.

docs.title: 2. Dependence measures
docs.text:
Concordance.

\[ au = 4\int_{[0,1]^2} C\,dC - 1, \qquad ho_S = 12\int_{[0,1]^2} C(u,v)\,du\,dv - 3 . \]

Tail dependence is the probability of joint extremes:

\[ \lambda_L = \lim_{q\downarrow0} rac{C(q,q)}{q}, \qquad \lambda_U = \lim_{q\uparrow1} rac{1 - 2q + C(q,q)}{1-q}. \]

Tail dependence is what separates the families in risk applications. The Gaussian copula is asymptotically independent in both tails whenever \(| ho| < 1\): joint crashes become rare in the limit, however high the correlation. This is a well-known limitation in credit and stress testing.

Copula Parameter Kendall's \( au\) \(\lambda_L\) \(\lambda_U\) Gaussian \( ho\) \( rac{2}{\pi}\arcsin ho\) 0 0 Student-\(t\) \( ho,\ u\) \( rac{2}{\pi}\arcsin ho\) \(2\,t_{ u+1}\!\left(-\sqrt{ rac{( u+1)(1- ho)}{1+ ho}} ight)\) \(=\lambda_L\) Clayton \( heta>0\) \( rac{ heta}{ heta+2}\) \(2^{-1/ heta}\) 0 Gumbel \( heta\ge1\) \(1- rac1 heta\) 0 \(2-2^{1/ heta}\) Frank \( heta e0\) \(1 - rac4 heta ig(1 - D_1( heta) ig)\) 0 0 Joe \( heta\ge1\) \(1 + 4\int_0^1 rac{\varphi(t)}{\varphi'(t)}dt\) 0 \(2-2^{1/ heta}\) AMH \( heta\in[-1,1)\) closed form via \(\log(1- heta)\) and \(\operatorname{Li}_2\) 0 0 Galambos \( heta>0\) numerical 0 \(2^{-1/ heta}\) Hüsler–Reiss \( heta>0\) numerical 0 \(2\,\Phi(-1/ heta)\)

Here \(D_1( heta) = rac1 heta\int_0^ heta rac{t}{e^t-1}dt\) is the Debye function. The kendall_tau(), spearman_rho() and tail_dependence() methods return these quantities. Where the right-hand column has a closed form, it is the one used.

docs.title: 3.1 Elliptical copulas
docs.text:
Elliptical copulas are extracted from elliptical distributions with correlation matrix \(R\):

\[ C^{ ext{Ga}}_R(u) = \Phi_R ig(\Phi^{-1}(u_1),\dots,\Phi^{-1}(u_d) ig), \qquad C^{t}_{R, u}(u) = t_{R, u} ig(t_ u^{-1}(u_1),\dots,t_ u^{-1}(u_d) ig). \]

They support any dimension and any valid correlation matrix. A supplied matrix is checked for symmetry, unit diagonal and positive definiteness. The relation \( au = rac2\pi\arcsin ho\) holds for every elliptical copula, so \( ho\) can be estimated robustly from Kendall's \( au\). The Student-\(t\) copula adds symmetric tail dependence, controlled by \( u\). As \( u o\infty\) it reduces to the Gaussian copula.

docs.title: 3.2 Archimedean copulas
docs.text:
An Archimedean copula is generated by a completely monotone generator \(\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]\) (the inverse of \(\varphi = \psi^{-1}\)):

\[ C(u) = \psi\big(\varphi(u_1) + \cdots + \varphi(u_d)\big). \] Family Generator \(\varphi(t)\) Clayton \(\frac1\theta(t^{-\theta}-1)\) Gumbel \((-\log t)^\theta\) Frank \(-\log\frac{e^{-\theta t}-1}{e^{-\theta}-1}\) Joe \(-\log\big(1-(1-t)^\theta\big)\) AMH \(\log\frac{1-\theta(1-t)}{t}\)

For Archimedean copulas, Kendall's \(\tau\) reduces to a one-dimensional integral (Genest & MacKay 1986):

\[ \tau = 1 + 4\int_0^1 \frac{\varphi(t)}{\varphi'(t)}\,dt . \]

Sampling is done by conditional inversion: draw \(u_1, w \sim U(0,1)\) and set \(u_2 = C_{2|1}^{-1}(w\mid u_1)\). The inverse is closed-form for Clayton and Frank and numerical otherwise. Gumbel uses the stable-mixture (Marshall–Olkin) representation.

docs.title: 3.3 Extreme-value copulas
docs.text:
Extreme-value copulas are the possible limits of copulas of componentwise maxima. In two dimensions they are characterised by a convex Pickands dependence function \(A:[0,1]\to[\tfrac12,1]\) with \(\max(t,1-t)\le A(t)\le 1\):

\[ C(u,v) = \exp\!\Big(\log(uv)\,A\Big(\frac{\log v}{\log(uv)}\Big)\Big), \qquad \lambda_U = 2\big(1 - A(\tfrac12)\big). \]

ExtremeValueCopula.pickands_a evaluates \(A\) for Galambos, \(A(t) = 1 - (t^{-\theta} + (1-t)^{-\theta})^{-1/\theta}\), and for Hüsler–Reiss, \(A(t) = (1-t)\,\Phi\big(\frac1\theta + \frac\theta2\log\frac{1-t}{t}\big) + t\,\Phi\big(\frac1\theta + \frac\theta2\log\frac{t}{1-t}\big)\).

docs.title: 3.4 Rosenblatt transform
docs.text:
The Rosenblatt transform maps \(U\sim C\) to independent uniforms:

\[ W_1 = U_1,\quad W_2 = C_{2|1}(U_2\mid U_1),\quad\dots \]

Here \(C_{2|1}(v\mid u) = \partial_u C(u,v)\) (conditional_cdf). The inverse transform (inverse_rosenblatt_transform) is the generic sampler. The forward transform is the basis of goodness-of-fit tests: transformed data should be i.i.d. uniform.

docs.title: 4. Estimation
docs.text:
The marginals are usually unknown or misspecified, so dependence is estimated from pseudo-observations (ranks):

\[ \hat U_{ij} = \frac{\operatorname{rank}(X_{ij})}{n+1} \]

(pseudo_observations). This makes estimation of \(C\) independent of any marginal model. fit_copula(u, family, method) supports two methods.

  • Canonical maximum likelihood (method="cml", Genest, Ghoudi & Rivest 1995). This maximises \(\sum_i \log c(\hat U_i;\theta)\). The estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, but not fully efficient, because the marginals are estimated nonparametrically.
  • Inversion of Kendall's \(\tau\) (method="itau", bivariate only). This solves \(\tau(\theta) = \hat\tau_n\), in closed form where possible (Clayton, Gumbel, elliptical) and by root-finding otherwise (Frank). For the Student-\(t\) copula only \(\rho\) is identified by \(\tau\), so \(\nu\) is fixed at 4. Fit \(\nu\) by CML instead. The method is robust and cheap, and makes a good starting value for maximum likelihood.

select_best_copula fits a list of candidate families by CML and ranks them by \(\text{AIC} = 2k - 2\log\hat L\). The candidates should include at least one family with lower and one with upper tail dependence, so that the choice is driven by the data and not by the candidate set.

docs.title: 5. Coupled processes
docs.text:
CoupledProcess(processes, copula) simulates \(d\) univariate zoo processes jointly. At every time step it draws \(U\sim C\), maps it to Gaussian drivers \(Z_j = \Phi^{-1}(U_j)\), and uses \(Z_j\) as the diffusive innovation of marginal \(j\). This leaves each marginal's one-step diffusive law unchanged while imposing the copula on the innovations. The class also provides Monte Carlo prices for multi-asset payoffs: basket_call_price, worst_of_call_price, best_of_call_price and spread_option_price.

Which object carries the copula

The copula is imposed on one-step innovations, not on the joint law of the terminal values. Aggregating many increments changes the dependence structure. By the multivariate central limit theorem, the copula of \((X^1_T, X^2_T)\) for diffusive marginals tends towards a Gaussian copula with correlation equal to the innovation correlation \(\operatorname{Corr}(Z_1,Z_2)\). Most of the tail dependence of a Clayton or Gumbel innovation copula therefore disappears over long horizons. To control the dependence of terminal values directly, sample \(U\sim C\) once and apply the marginal quantile functions of \(X^j_T\).

Scope of the marginal dynamics

CoupledProcess.simulate currently has explicit dynamics for Brownian, CIR (full-truncation Euler), Merton and Kou jump-diffusion marginals. Jump arrivals are independent across assets. Heston and Bates marginals are stepped with their variance frozen at \(\sqrt{v_0}\). Any other process type silently falls back to a geometric Euler step with a hard-coded 5% drift and 20% volatility that ignore the process's own parameters. Results for such marginals are wrong. Simulate them individually and couple their innovations explicitly.

docs.title: Information Geometry of Statistical Models
docs.text:
A parametric family of probability laws \(\{p(\cdot\,;\theta) : \theta \in \Theta \subset \mathbb{R}^n\}\) is a smooth manifold. If the score vectors are linearly independent, it carries a canonical Riemannian metric, the Fisher information metric. Because the metric is invariant under reparametrisation, distances, geodesics and curvature describe the model and do not depend on the coordinates chosen. spxa.geom provides these objects for the laws of stochastic processes. They are the foundation of geodesic model morphing (Model Morphing §3) and natural-gradient calibration.

Object Implementation Fisher metric \(g_{ij}(\theta)\) spxa.geom.FisherInformationMetric Levi-Civita and Amari \(\alpha\)-connections, curvature spxa.geom.AffineConnection Geodesics, exponential map, Rao distance spxa.geom.GeodesicFlow Natural-gradient descent on the DAG spxa.graph.geom.NaturalGradientCalibratorNode

docs.title: 1. The Fisher information metric
docs.text:
Let \(\ell(\theta) = \log p(X;\theta)\). Under the usual regularity conditions (differentiation under the integral sign is allowed), the score has mean zero and

\[ g_{ij}(\theta) \;=\; \mathbb{E}_\theta\!\left[\partial_i \ell \,\partial_j \ell\right] \;=\; -\,\mathbb{E}_\theta\!\left[\partial_i \partial_j \ell\right]. \]

\(g\) is symmetric positive semi-definite, and positive definite exactly when the model is locally identifiable. By the Čencov theorem, it is (up to scale) the only Riemannian metric on statistical manifolds that is invariant under sufficient statistics (Markov morphisms). FisherInformationMetric.is_positive_definite checks the identifiability condition numerically.

docs.title: 1.1 Univariate Gaussian
docs.text:
In coordinates \(\theta = (\mu, \sigma)\):

\[ g(\mu,\sigma) = \begin{pmatrix} 1/\sigma^2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2/\sigma^2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad ds^2 = \frac{d\mu^2 + 2\,d\sigma^2}{\sigma^2}. \]

Substituting \(\mu = \sqrt{2}\,x\) gives \(ds^2 = 2\,(dx^2 + d\sigma^2)/\sigma^2\), which is twice the Poincaré half-plane metric. The manifold is therefore a hyperbolic plane with constant Gaussian curvature \(K = -\tfrac12\) and scalar curvature \(R = 2K = -1\). AffineConnection.ricci_scalar reproduces \(R = -1\) to about \(10^{-7}\) at every point.

docs.title: 1.2 Gaussian transition densities (Ornstein–Uhlenbeck)
docs.text:
For any model whose likelihood is Gaussian, \(X \sim \mathcal{N}(m(\theta), v(\theta))\), the Fisher metric is

\[ g_{ij} = \frac{\partial_i m\,\partial_j m}{v} + \frac{\partial_i v\,\partial_j v}{2v^2}. \]

FisherInformationMetric.ou_transition_fisher applies this formula to the exact OU transition \(X_{\Delta}\mid X_0 = x_0\) of \(dX_t = \theta(\mu - X_t)\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t\), where

\[ m = x_0 e^{-\theta\Delta} + \mu(1 - e^{-\theta\Delta}),\qquad v = \frac{\sigma^2}{2\theta}\left(1 - e^{-2\theta\Delta}\right), \]

in coordinates \((\theta, \mu, \sigma)\). The information of \(N\) independent transitions is the sum of the per-transition matrices.

docs.title: 1.3 Empirical and observed information
docs.text:
When no closed form exists:

  • empirical_fisher(scores) returns \(\frac1N\sum_k s_k s_k^\top\) with \(s_k = \nabla_\theta \log p(x_k;\theta)\), the outer-product-of-gradients estimator.
  • numerical_hessian_fisher(nll, theta) returns the central-difference Hessian of the negative log-likelihood. This is the observed information, which is consistent for \(g\) at the MLE.

If the model is misspecified the two estimators differ, and the sandwich covariance of Calibration §4 should be used.

docs.title: 2.1 Levi-Civita connection
docs.text:
The Christoffel symbols of the second kind are

\[ \Gamma^k_{ij} = \tfrac12\, g^{kl}\left(\partial_i g_{jl} + \partial_j g_{il} - \partial_l g_{ij}\right). \]

AffineConnection(metric_fn, dim) computes them by central differences of a user-supplied metric \(\theta \mapsto g(\theta)\). The result has shape (dim, dim, dim), and index (k, i, j) is \(\Gamma^k_{ij}\).

docs.title: 2.2 Amari \(\alpha\)-connections
docs.text:
Statistical manifolds carry a one-parameter family of torsion-free connections (Amari & Nagaoka 2000):

\[ \Gamma^{(\alpha),k}_{ij} = \Gamma^k_{ij} - \frac{\alpha}{2}\, g^{kl}\, T_{ijl}, \qquad T_{ijl} = \mathbb{E}_\theta\!\left[\partial_i \ell\,\partial_j \ell\,\partial_l \ell\right]. \]
  • \(\alpha = 0\) gives the Levi-Civita connection, which is metric-compatible.
  • \(\alpha = 1\) gives the e-connection, which is flat for exponential families. Natural parameters are affine coordinates.
  • \(\alpha = -1\) gives the m-connection, which is flat for mixture families. Expectation parameters are affine coordinates.

The \(\pm\alpha\) connections are dual with respect to \(g\): \(\partial_k g_{ij} = \Gamma^{(\alpha)}_{ki,j} + \Gamma^{(-\alpha)}_{kj,i}\). This duality underlies the generalised Pythagorean theorem for KL divergence. Pass the skewness tensor \(T\) to amari_alpha_connection(theta, alpha, skewness_tensor).

docs.title: 2.3 Curvature
docs.text:
\[ R^l{}_{ijk} = \partial_j \Gamma^l_{ik} - \partial_k \Gamma^l_{ij} + \Gamma^m_{ik}\Gamma^l_{jm} - \Gamma^m_{ij}\Gamma^l_{km}, \qquad R_{ik} = R^l{}_{ilk},\qquad R = g^{ik}R_{ik}. \]

Curvature measures how far the model is from being flat. With negative curvature, as on the Gaussian manifold, geodesics diverge. Linear interpolation of parameters then differs noticeably from the geodesic, and the Fréchet mean of several models is unique.

docs.title: 3. Geodesics and Rao distance
docs.text:
A geodesic \(\theta(t)\) solves

\[ \ddot\theta^k + \Gamma^k_{ij}(\theta)\,\dot\theta^i\dot\theta^j = 0 . \]

GeodesicFlow integrates this equation as a first-order system in \((\theta, \dot\theta)\) using adaptive RK45.

  • Exponential map. exponential_map(theta0, v0) returns \(\operatorname{Exp}_{\theta_0}(v_0) = \theta(1)\) together with the whole trajectory.
  • Logarithm by shooting. geodesic_shooting(theta0, theta1) solves the two-point boundary value problem \(\theta(0)=\theta_0,\ \theta(1)=\theta_1\). It minimises \(\|\operatorname{Exp}_{\theta_0}(v) - \theta_1\|^2\) over \(v\), starting from the Euclidean guess \(v = \theta_1 - \theta_0\).
  • Rao distance. $\(d_R(\theta_0,\theta_1) = \int_0^1 \sqrt{g_{ij}(\theta(t))\,\dot\theta^i\dot\theta^j}\,dt .\)$ Speed is conserved along a geodesic, so this equals \(\sqrt{v_0^\top g(\theta_0) v_0}\). The trapezoidal integral therefore also measures the integrator's accuracy.

docs.title: Closed form on the Gaussian manifold
docs.text:
Using the half-plane isometry of §1.1,

\[ d_R\big((\mu_0,\sigma_0),(\mu_1,\sigma_1)\big) = \sqrt2\,\ln\frac{1+\delta}{1-\delta} = 2\sqrt2\,\operatorname{artanh}\delta, \qquad \delta = \sqrt{\frac{(\mu_1-\mu_0)^2 + 2(\sigma_1-\sigma_0)^2}{(\mu_1-\mu_0)^2 + 2(\sigma_1+\sigma_0)^2}} . \]

This is GeodesicFlow.gaussian_exact_rao_distance (and spxa.morph.gaussian_rao_distance). Geodesics are semi-ellipses centred on the \(\mu\)-axis (vertical lines when \(\mu_0=\mu_1\)). Along them a change of mean is "paid for" by a temporary increase in volatility.

import numpy as np
from spxa.geom import FisherInformationMetric, AffineConnection, GeodesicFlow

conn = AffineConnection(lambda th: FisherInformationMetric.gaussian_fisher(th[0], th[1]), dim=2)
flow = GeodesicFlow(conn)

print(conn.ricci_scalar(np.array([0.3, 1.2])))                        # ≈ -1.0
print(flow.rao_distance(np.array([0.0, 1.0]), np.array([1.0, 2.0])))  # ≈ 1.18936 (shooting)
print(GeodesicFlow.gaussian_exact_rao_distance((0.0, 1.0), (1.0, 2.0)))  # 1.18938 (closed form)

docs.title: 4. Natural-gradient calibration
docs.text:
For a loss \(\mathcal{L}( heta)\) on a statistical manifold, the direction of steepest descent with respect to the Fisher metric is the natural gradient (Amari 1998):

\[ ilde abla_ heta \mathcal{L} = g( heta)^{-1} abla_ heta \mathcal{L}, \qquad heta_{k+1} = heta_k - \eta\,(g( heta_k) + \lambda I)^{-1} abla_ heta \mathcal{L}( heta_k). \]

The update is invariant to smooth reparametrisation, to first order in \(\eta\). When \(\mathcal{L}\) is a negative log-likelihood, the natural gradient step with \(\eta = 1\) is Fisher scoring. NaturalGradientCalibratorNode implements the damped update above. It takes Tikhonov damping \(\lambda\), central-difference Euclidean gradients and parameter-bound clipping, and works on the ParameterNodes of a computational graph.

docs.title: The central bijection
docs.text:
A stochastic process \(X = (X_t)_{t \geq 0}\) is a Lévy process if it satisfies:

  1. \(X_0 = 0\) almost surely
  2. Independent increments: for \(0 \leq s < t\), \(X_t - X_s\) is independent of \(\mathcal{F}_s\)
  3. Stationary increments: \(X_t - X_s \sim X_{t-s}\) in distribution
  4. Stochastic continuity: \(\lim_{s \to t} P(|X_s - X_t| > \varepsilon) = 0\) for all \(\varepsilon > 0\)
  5. Càdlàg paths: right-continuous with left limits almost surely

The foundational result (Lévy 1934, Khintchine 1938) is a bijection:

\[\text{Lévy processes on } \mathbb{R}^d \longleftrightarrow \text{Infinitely divisible distributions on } \mathbb{R}^d\]

A distribution \(\mu\) is infinitely divisible if for every \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) there exist i.i.d. \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) with \(X_1 + \cdots + X_n \sim \mu\).

Given a Lévy process \(X\), the distribution of \(X_1\) is infinitely divisible. Conversely, given any infinitely divisible distribution \(\mu\), there exists a unique (in law) Lévy process with \(\mathcal{L}(X_1) = \mu\).

docs.title: The Lévy–Khintchine formula
docs.text:
Every Lévy process \(X\) on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) has characteristic function

\[\mathbb{E}\left[e^{i\langle u, X_t angle} ight] = e^{t \psi(u)}, \quad u \in \mathbb{R}^d\]

where the characteristic exponent \(\psi : \mathbb{R}^d o \mathbb{C}\) takes the form

\[\psi(u) = i\langle b, u angle - rac{1}{2}\langle u, \Sigma u angle + \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \left(e^{i\langle u, x angle} - 1 - i\langle u, x angle \mathbf{1}_{\|x\| \leq 1} ight) u(dx)\]

The triple \((b, \Sigma, u)\) is the Lévy–Khintchine triplet (or characteristic triplet) of \(X\), where:

  • \(b \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is the drift vector
  • \(\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{d imes d}\) is a symmetric positive semidefinite diffusion matrix; in one dimension this is \(\sigma^2 \geq 0\)
  • \( u\) is the Lévy measure on \(\mathbb{R}^d \setminus \{0\}\), satisfying \(\int (1 \wedge \|x\|^2)\, u(dx) < \infty\)

The representation is unique: two Lévy processes have the same law if and only if their triplets are identical (Sato 1999, Theorem 8.1).

docs.title: The Lévy–Itô decomposition
docs.text:
The triplet has a constructive interpretation. Every Lévy process decomposes as

\[X_t = bt + \sigma W_t + \int_{\|x\| > 1} x\, N(ds, dx) \cdot t + \int_{\|x\| \leq 1} x\, \tilde{N}(ds, dx)\]

where \(W\) is a standard Brownian motion, \(N\) is the Poisson random measure of jumps of \(X\), and \(\tilde{N}(ds, dx) = N(ds, dx) - \nu(dx)\, ds\) is the compensated measure. The four components are independent.

The Lévy measure \(\nu(B) = \mathbb{E}[\#\{t \in [0,1] : \Delta X_t \in B\}]\) counts the expected number of jumps per unit time of size in \(B\). It encodes the entire jump structure of the process.

docs.title: The truncation function
docs.text: The centering term \(\mathbf{1}_{\|x\| \leq 1}\) is a choice of truncation function. Different choices give different values of \(b\) but the same \(\Sigma\) and \(\nu\), so the triplet is only canonical relative to a fixed truncation. spxa uses \(h(x) = \mathbf{1}_{\|x\| \leq 1}\) throughout. When accepting external triplets from the literature, verify the truncation convention.

docs.title: Cumulants from the triplet
docs.text:
The \(n\)-th cumulant of \(X_t\) (when it exists) is \(t\) times the \(n\)-th cumulant of \(X_1\). For \(X_1\):

\[\kappa_1 = b + \int_{\|x\| > 1} x\, u(dx)\] \[\kappa_2 = \sigma^2 + \int x^2\, u(dx)\] \[\kappa_n = \int x^n\, u(dx), \quad n \geq 3\]

These exist if and only if \(\int_{\|x\| > 1} \|x\|^n\, u(dx) < \infty\). The Lévy measure's tail behavior completely controls the existence of moments.

docs.title: Infinite divisibility of the triplet
docs.text:
The set of valid triplets is closed under:

  • Convex combination of Lévy measures: \( u = \lambda u_1 + (1-\lambda) u_2\) with \(\lambda \in [0,1]\)
  • Scaling of \(b\) and \(\sigma^2\) by positive constants
  • Image measures: if \(T : \mathbb{R}^d o \mathbb{R}^k\) is linear, the image of a Lévy process under \(T\) is a Lévy process with triplet \((Tb, T\Sigma T^ op, u \circ T^{-1})\)

These are the mathematical facts that make spxa's arithmetic exact.
