docs.title: Model Morphing: Homotopies, Geodesics & Optimal Transport on Stochastic Processes
docs.text:
Stochastic modeling in finance, physics, and machine learning frequently confronts competing candidate models, non-stationary market regimes, and structural breaks. Traditional frameworks force a discrete choice between alternative models (e.g. Black-Scholes vs. Heston vs. Merton jump-diffusion) or rely on discontinuous regime switching.

The Model Morphing Framework (spxa.morph) establishes a unified mathematical foundation for continuous homotopies, information-geometric geodesics, and optimal transport displacement interpolations across stochastic processes:

\[P_\alpha = \text{Morph}(P_0, P_1; \alpha), \quad \alpha \in [0, 1]\]

docs.title: 1. Characteristic Triplet Morphing
docs.text:
On the cone of conditionally positive-definite continuous functions (the space of Lévy-Khintchine exponents), convex combinations preserve infinite divisibility (Sato 1999, Theorem 8.1).

For two Lévy processes \(X_0 \sim (b_0, \sigma_0^2, u_0)\) and \(X_1 \sim (b_1, \sigma_1^2, u_1)\):

\[\psi_\alpha(u) = (1 - \alpha) \psi_0(u) + \alpha \psi_1(u)\]

The corresponding characteristic triplet \((b_\alpha, \sigma_\alpha^2, u_\alpha)\) satisfies:

\[b_\alpha = (1 - \alpha) b_0 + \alpha b_1$$ $$\sigma_\alpha^2 = (1 - \alpha) \sigma_0^2 + \alpha \sigma_1^2$$ $$ u_\alpha(dx) = (1 - \alpha) u_0(dx) + \alpha u_1(dx)\]

Because infinite divisibility and the Lévy-Khintchine representation are strictly preserved, if both parent processes possess ExactnessLevel.EXACT, the morphed process is mathematically exact:

\[\mathbb{E}[e^{iu X_\alpha(t)}] = (\mathbb{E}[e^{iu X_0(t)}])^{1 - \alpha} \cdot (\mathbb{E}[e^{iu X_1(t)}])^\alpha\]

Cumulants scale linearly:

\[\kappa_n(X_\alpha(1)) = (1 - \alpha) \kappa_n(X_0(1)) + \alpha \kappa_n(X_1(1))\]

docs.title: 2. Infinitesimal Generator Homotopy
docs.text:
For Markov diffusions and jump-diffusions, morphing operates on the infinitesimal generator:

\[\mathcal{A}_\alpha = (1 - \alpha) \mathcal{A}_0 + \alpha \mathcal{A}_1\]

Applied to test functions \(f \in C_b^2(\mathbb{R})\):

\[\mathcal{A}_\alpha f(x) = \mu_\alpha(t, x) f'(x) + \frac{1}{2} \sigma_\alpha^2(t, x) f''(x) + \int_{\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}} [f(x + z) - f(x) - z f'(x) \mathbf{1}_{|z| \le 1}] J_\alpha(x, dz)\]

with:

\[\mu_\alpha(t, x) = (1 - \alpha) \mu_0(t, x) + \alpha \mu_1(t, x)$$ $$\sigma_\alpha(t, x) = \sqrt{(1 - \alpha) \sigma_0^2(t, x) + \alpha \sigma_1^2(t, x)}\]

docs.title: 3. Information-Geometric Geodesics
docs.text:
A parametric model family forms a Riemannian manifold equipped with the Fisher-Rao metric tensor:

\[g_{ij}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}\left[ \frac{\partial \ln p(x; \theta)}{\partial \theta^i} \frac{\partial \ln p(x; \theta)}{\partial \theta^j} \right]\]

Morphing from \(\theta_0\) to \(\theta_1\) follows the geodesic \(\theta(\alpha)\) minimizing the Rao action:

\[\frac{d^2 \theta^k}{d\alpha^2} + \Gamma^k_{ij}(\theta(\alpha)) \frac{d\theta^i}{d\alpha} \frac{d\theta^j}{d\alpha} = 0\]

For Gaussian diffusions \(\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), the Fisher-Rao geometry is isometric to the Poincaré half-plane \(\mathbb{H}^2\):

\[ds^2 = \frac{d\mu^2 + 2 d\sigma^2}{\sigma^2}\]

with exact Rao distance:

\[d_R(\theta_0, \theta_1) = \sqrt{2} \ln\left( \frac{1 + \delta}{1 - \delta} \right), \quad \delta = \sqrt{ \frac{(\mu_1 - \mu_0)^2 + 2(\sigma_1 - \sigma_0)^2}{(\mu_1 - \mu_0)^2 + 2(\sigma_1 + \sigma_0)^2} }\]

docs.title: 4. Optimal Transport & McCann Displacement Interpolation
docs.text:
In the 2-Wasserstein metric space \((\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R}^d), W_2)\), the constant-speed geodesic between measures \(\mu_0\) and \(\mu_1\) is given by McCann's displacement interpolation:

\[\mu_\alpha = ((1 - \alpha) \text{id} + \alpha T)_\# \mu_0\]

where \(T\) is the Brenier optimal transport map. In 1D, quantile functions morph with linear interpolation:

\[F_\alpha^{-1}(u) = (1 - \alpha) F_0^{-1}(u) + \alpha F_1^{-1}(u), \quad u \in (0, 1)\]

For multi-dimensional Gaussians \(\mathcal{N}(m_k, \Sigma_k)\), displacement interpolation yields:

\[m_\alpha = (1 - \alpha) m_0 + \alpha m_1$$ $$\Sigma_\alpha = ((1 - \alpha) I + \alpha A) \Sigma_0 ((1 - \alpha) I + \alpha A)^\top\]

where \(A = \Sigma_0^{-1/2} (\Sigma_0^{1/2} \Sigma_1 \Sigma_0^{1/2})^{1/2} \Sigma_0^{-1/2}\).

docs.title: 5. Arbitrage-Free Implied Volatility Surface Morphing
docs.text:
When morphing implied volatility surfaces, total implied variance \(w(k, T) = \sigma_{\text{IV}}^2(k, T) \cdot T\) is interpolated:

\[w_\alpha(k, T) = (1 - \alpha) w_0(k, T) + \alpha w_1(k, T)\]

No-arbitrage conditions along the morphing path: 1. Calendar Spread Arbitrage Absence: $\(\partial_T w_\alpha(k, T) = (1 - \alpha) \partial_T w_0(k, T) + \alpha \partial_T w_1(k, T) \ge 0\)$ 2. Butterfly Arbitrage Absence (Gatheral-Jacquier Condition): $\(g_\alpha(k, T) = \left( 1 - \frac{k w'}{2w} \right)^2 - \frac{w'}{4} \left( \frac{1}{w} + \frac{1}{4} \right) + \frac{w''}{2} \ge 0\)$

docs.title: PDE and PIDE Methods
docs.text:
Every Markov process in spxa has a generator \(\mathcal{A}\). By the Feynman–Kac theorem, a discounted expectation

\[ u(x, \tau) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[e^{-\int_0^\tau r\,ds}\, g(X_\tau) \,\middle|\, X_0 = x\right] \]

solves the backward equation \(u_\tau = \mathcal{A}u - r u\) with \(u(x, 0) = g(x)\). Here \(\tau = T - t\) is time to maturity. spxa.pde discretises these equations with finite differences. Every scheme in the package has a test that measures its convergence order against a closed form or a published reference.

Object Implementation Grids, boundary conditions, θ-stepping Grid1D, TimeGrid, Dirichlet/Neumann/Linear/Natural, ThetaSolver1D Early exercise (LCP) PenaltyLCP, PSORLCP, BrennanSchwartzLCP, IkonenToivanenLCP Black–Scholes and local volatility BlackScholesPDE, DupirePDE, DupireSurface Asian options AsianPDE (Večeř) Short-rate models ShortRatePDE Generators of zoo processes to_pde, DiffusionPDE, Process.to_pde() Transition densities FokkerPlanck1D, DensitySolution Exponential Lévy models LevyJumpOperator, LevyPIDE Two-factor problems (ADI) DiscreteOperator2D, ADISolver, HestonPDE, TwoAssetBlackScholesPDE Simulation cross-check longstaff_schwartz, lsm_american Bridges pde_price / pde_pricing_fn (spxa.risk), spxa.graph.pde nodes Verification convergence_study, observed_order, richardson_extrapolate, spxa.pde.reference

docs.title: 1.1 Equation and grids
docs.text:
Every one-dimensional problem has the form

\[ u_\tau = a(x,\tau)\,u_{xx} + b(x,\tau)\,u_x + c(x,\tau)\,u + f(x,\tau), \]

where \(a \ge 0\). Each coefficient can be a scalar, an array of nodal values, or a callable f(x, tau).

Grids. Grids are either uniform or sinh-stretched:

\[ x(\xi) = c + \alpha \sinh\!\big(c_2\xi + c_1(1-\xi)\big), \qquad \xi \in [0, 1], \]

with \(c_1 = \operatorname{arsinh}((x_{\min}-c)/\alpha)\) and \(c_2 = \operatorname{arsinh}((x_{\max}-c)/\alpha)\). This clusters nodes around the strike \(c\), and \(\alpha\) sets how strongly. Strikes, barriers and spots are placed exactly on nodes. The grid is split at each of these points in \(\xi\), and the nodes are spread in proportion to the lengths of the pieces. This keeps the spacing ratio at \(1 + O(1/n)\). Snapping a node onto the strike after the fact would instead perturb the local spacing by up to half a cell.

Stencils. First and second derivatives use three-point stencils that are exact for quadratics on non-uniform grids, so the scheme is second order. Where the cell Péclet number \(|b|h/(2a)\) exceeds one, the drift term can switch to an upwind stencil (convection_scheme='auto').

Boundary conditions. Four kinds are available:

  • Dirichlet: \(u = g(\tau)\).
  • Neumann: \(u_x = g(\tau)\).
  • Linear: \(u_{xx} = 0\), appropriate for far fields where the solution is asymptotically linear.
  • Natural: the equation itself, with one-sided derivatives. Use this on degenerate boundaries such as \(S = 0\), where \(a = b = 0\).

docs.title: 1.2 Time stepping
docs.text:
The solver uses the θ-scheme

\[ (I - \theta\Delta\tau A)\,U^{n+1} = (I + (1-\theta)\Delta\tau A)\,U^n + \Delta\tau\,(\theta F^{n+1} + (1-\theta)F^n). \]

It factorises each matrix once with sparse LU (splu) and reuses the factorisation while the coefficients stay constant. Crank–Nicolson (\(\theta = \frac12\)) is second order. However, the kink of a vanilla payoff excites the high-frequency modes that Crank–Nicolson does not damp. To control this, the solver first takes two fully implicit half-steps (Rannacher, 1984) and projects the payoff onto control-volume averages next to the kink. Together these restore second-order convergence for values and Greeks.

Events are specified in calendar time and converted with \(\tau = T - t\). They include:

  • discrete dividends, applied as the jump condition \(u(S) \leftarrow u(S - D)\) by cubic interpolation;
  • Bermudan exercise dates;
  • discrete barrier monitoring.

docs.title: 1.3 Early exercise
docs.text:
An American option solves the linear complementarity problem (LCP)

\[ u_\tau - \mathcal{L}u \ge 0,\qquad u \ge g,\qquad (u_\tau - \mathcal{L}u)(u - g) = 0. \]

After discretisation, each time step becomes a finite LCP \(Mu \ge q\), \(u \ge g\), \((Mu-q)^\top(u-g) = 0\). Four solvers are provided:

Solver Method PenaltyLCP Forsyth–Vetzal penalty iteration \((M + P(u))u = q + P(u)g\), with penalty \(1/\mathrm{tol}\) PSORLCP Projected SOR BrennanSchwartzLCP Direct elimination for tridiagonal \(M\) with a single exercise region on the given side IkonenToivanenLCP Operator splitting: \(\tilde u\) from the linear system with multiplier \(\lambda\); then \(u = \max(\tilde u - \Delta\tau\lambda, g)\) and \(\lambda \leftarrow \max(0, \lambda + (g - \tilde u)/\Delta\tau)\)

complementarity_residual measures how well a computed solution satisfies the LCP. The exercise boundary is recorded at every step and returned as an ExerciseBoundary.

docs.title: 1.4 Black–Scholes and its variants
docs.text:
BlackScholesPDE(r, sigma, q) solves the equation in \(S\) on \([0, S_{\max}]\) with

\[ S_{\max} = \max(S_0, K)\,e^{6\sigma\sqrt T}, \]

a natural boundary at \(S = 0\) and a linear boundary at \(S_{\max}\). The volatility \(\sigma\) can be a function \(\sigma(S, t)\) (local volatility). Supported contracts:

  • European, digital, American, Bermudan. Vega and rho are available by bump-and-revalue.
  • Barriers. Continuously monitored barriers end the computational domain, with a Dirichlet rebate there. Knock-ins use in–out parity: vanilla minus knock-out, plus the rebate times the price of a no-touch claim.
  • Double barriers and discretely monitored barriers. For discrete monitoring, the solution is reset to the rebate outside the barrier on each monitoring date.

Verification. The pricers are checked against:

  • the Black–Scholes formula, with second-order convergence of price, delta and gamma;
  • Reiner–Rubinstein barrier formulas and the sine-series double-barrier price;
  • the Broadie–Glasserman–Kou continuity correction and Fusai's discrete barrier values;
  • the Leisen–Reimer binomial tree for American options;
  • the perpetual put \(\frac{K}{1+\beta}\left(\frac{S}{S^*}\right)^{-\beta}\).

docs.title: 1.5 Local volatility (Dupire)
docs.text:
Call prices as a function of strike, \(C(K, T)\), satisfy the forward equation

\[ C_T = \tfrac12\sigma^2(K,T)K^2 C_{KK} - (r-q)K C_K - qC, \]

with \(C(K, 0) = (S_0 - K)^+\), \(C(0, T) = S_0e^{-qT}\) and \(C(K_{\max}, T) = 0\). DupirePDE prices a whole strike–maturity surface in a single solve. local_vol_from_prices inverts the relation numerically. In the tests, CEV prices from the non-central \(\chi^2\) formula are reproduced to about \(10^{-4}\).

docs.title: 1.6 Asian options (Večeř)
docs.text:
A fixed-strike Asian call on \(A = \frac1T\int_0^T S_t\,dt\) can be replicated by a self-financing portfolio that holds \(q_t\) shares of the underlying. For a continuous average,

\[ q_t = \frac{e^{-\delta(T-t)} - e^{-r(T-t)}}{(r-\delta)T}. \]

For a discrete average,

\[ q_t = \frac{e^{-r(T-t)}}{n}\sum_{t_i > t} e^{(r-\delta)(t_i - t)}. \]

Here \(\delta\) is the dividend yield. Measure the portfolio value in units of the dividend-reinvested asset \(S_te^{\delta t}\) and call the result \(z_t\). Then \(z_t\) is a driftless diffusion, \(dz = \sigma(\varphi_t - z)\,dW\) with \(\varphi_t = q_te^{-\delta t}\). The price is \(S_0u(0, z_0)\), where

\[ u_t + \tfrac12\sigma^2(\varphi_t - z)^2u_{zz} = 0,\qquad u(T, z) = z^+,\qquad z_0 = q_0 - e^{-rT}\frac{K - A_{\text{past}}}{S_0}. \]

Far from the kink, \(u \to 0\) as \(z \to -\infty\) and \(u \to z\) as \(z \to \infty\). These limits are imposed as Dirichlet conditions. For discrete averaging, \(q_t\) jumps at each fixing, so the equation is solved segment by segment between fixings. The tests reproduce Linetsky's spectral values to \(10^{-4}\).

docs.title: 1.7 Short rate
docs.text:
ShortRatePDE prices zero-coupon bonds, coupon bonds and European or American bond options. It solves

\[ u_\tau = \tfrac12\sigma^2r^{2\beta}u_{rr} + \kappa(\theta - r)u_r - ru, \]

with \(\beta = 0\) for Vasicek and \(\beta = \frac12\) for CIR. For CIR the domain starts at \(r = 0\), and the equation itself is the boundary condition there. A bond option is solved in two stages. First the bond is solved to its maturity \(S\). Then the option is solved to its expiry \(T\), with the payoff kink at \(r^*\) placed on a node. Vasicek option prices are checked against Jamshidian's formula with

\[ \sigma_p = \frac{\sigma}{\kappa}\big(1 - e^{-\kappa(S-T)}\big)\sqrt{\frac{1 - e^{-2\kappa T}}{2\kappa}}, \]

and agree to about \(10^{-6}\). CIR bond options are checked against the non-central \(\chi^2\) formula.

docs.title: 2. Generators and densities
docs.text:
to_pde(process) maps a zoo process to its pricing equation:

  • For a diffusion \(dX = \mu(X)\,dt + \sigma(X)\,dW\) it returns a DiffusionPDE with \(a = \frac12\sigma^2\) and \(b = \mu\).
  • For an exponential Lévy model it returns a LevyPIDE (Section 3). This requires the rate r.

Process.to_pde() delegates to the same function.

Fokker–Planck. The density \(p(x,t)\) of \(X_t\) solves the adjoint equation \(p_t = \mathcal{A}^*p\). FokkerPlanck1D does not discretise \(\mathcal{A}^*\) separately. Instead it uses the discrete adjoint of the backward operator,

\[ P = V^{-1}A^\top V, \]

where \(V\) holds the control-volume widths. Because \(\mathbf{1}^\top A = 0\) row-wise for a generator, this gives \(\frac{d}{dt}\sum_i V_ip_i = 0\), so total mass is conserved to machine precision. It also makes forward and backward prices consistent: \(\sum_i V_i p_i(T)\,g_i\) equals the backward solution at \(x_0\). The tests check Ornstein–Uhlenbeck and CIR densities in \(L^1\) (\(3\times10^{-5}\) for OU) and verify mass conservation to \(10^{-12}\).

docs.title: 3. Partial integro-differential equations
docs.text:
For \(S_t = S_0e^{X_t}\) with \(X\) a Lévy process with triplet \((b, \sigma^2, u)\), the price in \(x = \ln S\) solves

\[ u_ au = frac12\sigma^2 u_{xx} + \Big(r - q - frac12\sigma^2 - \omega\Big)u_x - ru + \int_{\mathbb{R}} ig[u(x+y) - u(x) ig]\, u(dy), \]

where \(\omega = \int (e^y - 1)\, u(dy)\) is the martingale correction. LevyJumpOperator discretises the integral term on a uniform grid with spacing \(h\). It treats jumps of different sizes differently:

  • Large jumps (\(|y| \ge h/2\)) use cell-integrated weights \( u([y_k - h/2, y_k + h/2])\). The convolution is computed with fftconvolve. Outside the domain, the solution is replaced by its asymptotic values.
  • Small jumps (\(|y| < h/2\)) are replaced by a diffusion with variance \(\int_{|y|<h/2} y^2\, u(dy)\) (Asmussen–Rosiński). For infinite-activity models this reduces the error from \(O(h^{2-Y})\) to \(O(h^2)\).
  • Interpolation error. The variance lost by representing jumps on the grid is matched exactly by an extra local diffusion. Pure-jump models can then have a negative net local coefficient; the operator is assembled directly so that this case is handled.

Time stepping and American options. The integral term is treated explicitly inside a fixed-point iteration around Crank–Nicolson with Rannacher start-up. Each step therefore needs only tridiagonal solves. American options combine the penalty iteration with the jump iteration. Alternatively, Ikonen–Toivanen can be applied once per step, which adds a splitting error of \(O(\Delta au)\).

Verification (n = 801):

Model Reference Error Merton put series \(9 imes10^{-5}\), second order Kou Kou (2002) closed form; Lewis formula for puts and Greeks \(\le 8 imes10^{-5}\) for calls Variance Gamma, CGMY (\(Y = 0.5, 1.5\)), NIG Lewis formula \(\le 3 imes10^{-4}\) American Merton puts d'Halluin–Forsyth–Labahn / compact-scheme references \(\le 1.4 imes10^{-4}\)

The Lewis formula used throughout is

\[ C = S e^{-qT} - rac{\sqrt{SK}\,e^{-(r+q)T/2}}{\pi}\int_0^\infty \operatorname{Re}\!\left[e^{iuk}\varphi_X(u - frac i2) ight] rac{du}{u^2 + rac14}, \qquad k = \ln(S/K) + (r-q)T. \]

docs.title: 4.1 Splitting
docs.text:
Two-factor problems have the form

\[ u_\tau = a_{xx}u_{xx} + a_{xy}u_{xy} + a_{yy}u_{yy} + b_xu_x + b_yu_y + cu + f. \]

They are discretised on a tensor grid with second-order stencils. The mixed derivative uses a nine-point stencil at interior nodes. DiscreteOperator2D splits the semi-discrete operator as

\[ A = A_0 + A_1 + A_2, \]

where \(A_0\) is the mixed term and \(A_1\), \(A_2\) are the \(x\) and \(y\) parts, each carrying half of \(c\). \(A_1\) is tridiagonal in \(x\) and \(A_2\) is tridiagonal in \(y\), so the implicit stages reduce to one-dimensional solves.

Edges can be Dirichlet2D, Neumann2D (ghost point), Natural2D (the equation with one-sided derivatives) or Linear2D (\(u_{nn} = 0\)). The mixed term is omitted on edges. This is exact whenever \(a_{xy}\) or \(u_{xy}\) vanishes there, which is the case for every edge used by the Heston and two-asset pricers.

docs.title: 4.2 Schemes
docs.text:
With \(F_j(t, U) = A_jU + b_j(t)\), the Douglas scheme is

\[ \begin{aligned} Y_0 &= U^n + \Delta t\,F(t_n, U^n),\\ Y_j &= Y_{j-1} + \theta\Delta t\big(F_j(t_{n+1}, Y_j) - F_j(t_n, U^n)\big),\qquad j = 1, 2. \end{aligned} \]

The Craig–Sneyd (CS), modified Craig–Sneyd (MCS) and Hundsdorfer–Verwer (HV) schemes add a correction stage and repeat the implicit sweeps. For HV, the second sweep is taken relative to \(Y_2\) at \(t_{n+1}\). ADISolver implements all four (in 't Hout & Welfert, 2007, 2009), with these defaults:

Scheme Default \(\theta\) Order with a mixed term Douglas \(\frac12\) 1 Craig–Sneyd \(\frac12\) 2 Modified Craig–Sneyd \(\frac13\) 2 Hundsdorfer–Verwer \(\frac12 + \frac{\sqrt3}{6}\) 2

As in one dimension, non-smooth payoffs are handled by first taking implicit damping steps (Douglas with \(\theta = 1\) on half-steps). Early exercise uses the Ikonen–Toivanen splitting: the multiplier enters the explicit stage, and the projection is applied after the step (Haentjens & in 't Hout, 2015).

The tests use the exact solution \(u = e^{\alpha x + \beta y + \gamma\tau}\) on stretched grids with a mixed term. They measure second order in space for CS, MCS and HV, and the time orders listed in the table above.

docs.title: 4.3 Heston
docs.text:
The Heston equation in \((S, v)\) is

\[ u_\tau = \tfrac12 S^2 v\,u_{SS} + \rho\sigma Sv\,u_{Sv} + \tfrac12\sigma^2v\,u_{vv} + (r-q)Su_S + \kappa(\theta - v)u_v - ru. \]

It is solved on \([0, 8K]\times[0, 5]\) with the boundary conditions of in 't Hout & Foulon (2010):

Edge Condition \(S = 0\) Dirichlet \(S_{\max}\) \(u_S = e^{-q\tau}\) (calls) or \(0\) (puts) \(v = 0\) The degenerate equation itself, with a one-sided \(u_v\) (no condition needed, whether or not the Feller condition holds) \(v_{\max}\) \(u_v = 0\)

The grids are sinh-stretched around the strike with \(c = K/5\), and around \(v = 0\) with \(d = v_{\max}/500\). Where convection in \(v\) dominates, the \(u_v\) stencil is upwinded at second order.

Verification:

  • Case 1 of in 't Hout–Foulon (\(\kappa = 1.5\), \(\theta = 0.04\), \(\sigma = 0.3\), \(\rho = -0.9\)): matches the Lewis price with second-order convergence, and errors below \(10^{-3}\) on \(201\times101\).
  • American puts: the Ikonen–Toivanen (2009) reference values (\(K = 10\), \(T = 0.25\), \(S = 8, \dots, 12\), \(v_0 = 0.0625\) and \(0.25\)) are reproduced within \(2\times10^{-4}\).

docs.title: 4.4 Two assets
docs.text:
TwoAssetBlackScholesPDE uses:

  • the equation itself on the axes, where the mixed term vanishes;
  • linear conditions on the far edges;
  • sinh grids around the spots.

Verification:

  • Margrabe's exchange option, with second-order convergence for \(\rho \in \{-0.6, 0, 0.5, 0.9\}\).
  • Spread options against a conditional (Gauss–Hermite) formula, which is itself checked against adaptive quadrature.
  • The identity best-of + worst-of = two vanilla calls.
  • A payoff that depends on one asset reproduces the Black–Scholes price.

docs.title: 5. Least-squares Monte Carlo
docs.text:
longstaff_schwartz estimates continuation values by regressing discounted cash flows on weighted Laguerre polynomials \(e^{-x/2}L_k(x)\) or on monomials, using in-the-money paths only.

In two-pass mode, the exercise rule is fitted on independent regression paths and then applied to the valuation paths. The resulting estimate is unbiased for a sub-optimal policy, so it is a lower bound in expectation and comes with an honest standard error. On the Longstaff–Schwartz test cases, it agrees with the Bermudan PDE value with the same 50 exercise dates to within three standard errors.

docs.title: 6. Using the results
docs.text:
Result objects. PDEPricingResult, HestonPDEResult, TwoAssetPDEResult, LSMResult, DensitySolution and PDEQuote all implement __story__(), which gives a plain-language account of the grid, the scheme and the Greeks. Solutions can be evaluated anywhere in the domain:

  • one dimension: cubic interpolation;
  • two dimensions: bicubic splines.

Greeks. Greeks come from the grid via three-point nodal stencils followed by interpolation. On a log grid, \(\Delta = u_x/S\) and \(\Gamma = (u_{xx} - u_x)/S^2\).

Bridges to the rest of spxa.

  • pde_price(instrument, market) values spxa.risk instruments. pde_pricing_fn(book) turns a book into the callable that StressTestingEngine expects.
  • spxa.graph.pde.bs_pde_price_node and heston_pde_price_node put PDE prices into computational graphs. Their vector–Jacobian products use the grid Greeks.

Convergence studies. convergence_study refines grids and reports observed orders and a Richardson-extrapolated value. It is the recommended way to confirm the accuracy of any new configuration.

docs.title: Rough Paths and Path Signatures
docs.text:
The signature of a path is the sequence of its iterated integrals. It is a graded, coordinate-free summary that determines the path up to tree-like equivalence (Hambly & Lyons 2010). It also linearises every continuous function of the path: any such function can be approximated by a linear functional of the signature. spxa.signature implements truncated signatures, the shuffle and Lie algebra structure, and the signature kernel computed by solving a Goursat PDE.

Object Implementation Truncated signature \(S^{(M)}(X)\), Chen products spxa.signature.PathSignature Shuffles, log-signature, Witt dimensions spxa.signature.SignatureAlgebra Signature kernel \(\langle S(X), S(Y)\rangle\) spxa.signature.SignatureKernel Graph nodes spxa.graph.signature.PathSignatureNode, SignatureKernelNode, ExpectedSignatureNode, SignatureLinearPricerNode

docs.title: 1. The tensor algebra and the signature
docs.text:
Let \(X:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^d\) have bounded variation. Its signature over \([s,t]\) is the element of the tensor algebra \(T((\mathbb{R}^d)) = \prod_{k\ge0}(\mathbb{R}^d)^{\otimes k}\)

\[ S(X)_{s,t} = \Big(1,\; \int_{s<u_1<t} dX_{u_1},\; \int_{s<u_1<u_2<t} dX_{u_1}\otimes dX_{u_2},\; \dots\Big). \]

Coordinate \((i_1,\dots,i_k)\) at level \(k\) is \(S^{i_1\cdots i_k}_{s,t} = \int_{s<u_1<\dots<u_k<t} dX^{i_1}_{u_1}\cdots dX^{i_k}_{u_k}\). Truncating at depth \(M\) leaves

\[ \dim T^{(M)}(\mathbb{R}^d) = \sum_{k=0}^M d^k = \frac{d^{M+1}-1}{d-1} \]

coordinates (PathSignature.signature_dimension). Levels are stored as flattened arrays in row-major (lexicographic word) order. For example, sig[2].reshape(d, d)[i, j] is \(S^{ij}\).

docs.title: 1.1 Linear segments
docs.text:
For a single linear segment with increment \(\Delta\), every iterated integral can be computed in closed form:

\[ S(\Delta) = \exp_\otimes(\Delta) = \sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\Delta^{\otimes k}}{k!}. \]

docs.title: 1.2 Chen's identity
docs.text:
Concatenating paths corresponds to multiplying their signatures in the tensor algebra:

\[ S(X)_{s,u} = S(X)_{s,t}\otimes S(X)_{t,u}, \qquad (A\otimes B)^{(k)} = \sum_{j=0}^k A^{(j)}\otimes B^{(k-j)} . \]

PathSignature.signature evaluates the signature of a piecewise-linear interpolation of the sample points exactly, as the product \(\bigotimes_i \exp_\otimes(\Delta X_i)\). verify_chen_identity checks the identity numerically by splitting a path. No discretisation error is introduced. The only approximation is the piecewise-linear interpolation of the data.

docs.title: 1.3 Properties used in practice
docs.text:
• Invariance under reparametrisation. \(S(X\circ\phi) = S(X)\) for increasing \(\phi\), so the signature ignores the speed at which a path is traversed. To keep time information, add time as an extra coordinate: \(\hat X_t = (t, X_t)\).
  • Uniqueness. Up to tree-like equivalence, \(S(X)\) determines \(X\). For time-augmented paths it determines \(X\) exactly.
  • Universality. On compact sets of paths, linear functionals \(\langle \ell, S(X)\rangle\) are dense in the continuous functions. This is why signature regression works for path-dependent payoffs.
  • Factorial decay. \(\|S^{(k)}(X)\| \le \|X\|_{1\text{-var}}^k / k!\), so truncation error decays super-exponentially in \(M\).

docs.title: 2.1 Shuffle identity
docs.text:
For words \(u, v\), the shuffle product \(u \sqcup\!\sqcup\, v\) is the sum of all interleavings that keep the order within \(u\) and within \(v\) (SignatureAlgebra.shuffles). The signature is a character of the shuffle algebra:

\[ \langle S(X), u\rangle\,\langle S(X), v\rangle = \langle S(X), u \sqcup\!\sqcup\, v\rangle . \]

In particular \(S^i S^j = S^{ij} + S^{ji}\). Products of signature coordinates are therefore again linear in the signature, which is the algebraic basis of universality.

docs.title: 2.2 Group-like elements and the free Lie algebra
docs.text:
Signatures are group-like: \(\log_\otimes S(X)\) lies in the free Lie algebra \(\mathfrak{g}(\mathbb{R}^d)\), the space spanned by iterated commutators \([e_i, e_j] = e_i\otimes e_j - e_j\otimes e_i\). Up to level 3,

\[ \log S = S^{(1)} + \Big(S^{(2)} - \tfrac12 S^{(1)}\otimes S^{(1)}\Big) + \Big(S^{(3)} - \tfrac12\big(S^{(1)}\otimes S^{(2)} + S^{(2)}\otimes S^{(1)}\big) + \tfrac13 (S^{(1)})^{\otimes3}\Big) + \cdots \]

For \(d = 2\), SignatureAlgebra.log_signature_2d returns coordinates in the Hall basis:

Level Basis Coordinate 1 \(e_1, e_2\) \(S^1, S^2\) (total increment) 2 \([e_1,e_2]\) Lévy area \(A^{12} = \tfrac12(S^{12}-S^{21})\) 3 \([[e_1,e_2],e_1],\ [[e_1,e_2],e_2]\) \(\tfrac16\langle S^{(3)}, 2\cdot121 - 112 - 211\rangle,\ \tfrac16\langle S^{(3)}, 122 - 2\cdot212 + 221\rangle\)

The level-3 formulas rely on two facts. First, \(\langle S, P\rangle = \langle\log S, P\rangle\) for every Lie polynomial \(P\). Second, the two level-3 basis polynomials are orthogonal, each with squared norm 6. The test suite checks the reconstruction \(\log S^{(3)} = c_1[[e_1,e_2],e_1] + c_2[[e_1,e_2],e_2]\) against the tensor logarithm to machine precision.

docs.title: 2.3 Witt's formula
docs.text:
The dimension of the level-\(k\) component of the free Lie algebra on \(d\) generators is the necklace polynomial

\[ L_d(k) = \frac1k\sum_{m\mid k}\mu(m)\, d^{k/m}, \]

where \(\mu\) is the Möbius function. log_signature_dimension(d, M) returns \(\sum_{k\le M}L_d(k)\). For \(d=2\) the level dimensions are \(2,1,2,3,6,9,18,30,56,99,\dots\), so at depth 10 the log-signature has 226 coordinates against 2046 for the signature.

docs.title: 3. The signature kernel
docs.text:
For paths \(X\) and \(Y\), the signature kernel \(K(X,Y) = \langle S(X), S(Y)\rangle\) (using the inner product induced by the Euclidean inner product on each level) solves a linear hyperbolic Goursat problem (Salvi, Cass, Foster, Lyons & Yang 2021):

\[ \frac{\partial^2 K}{\partial s\,\partial t}(s,t) = \langle \dot X_s, \dot Y_t\rangle\, K(s,t), \qquad K(s,0) = K(0,t) = 1, \]

and \(K(X,Y) = K(T_X, T_Y)\). This is the untruncated inner product, and evaluating it costs \(O(NM\,d)\) for paths with \(N\) and \(M\) segments.

docs.title: 3.1 Discretisation
docs.text:
For piecewise-linear paths, \(\langle\dot X,\dot Y\rangle\) is constant on each grid cell, with cell value \(M_{ij} = \langle\Delta X_i, \Delta Y_j\rangle\) after scaling to unit cells. Integrating the PDE over a cell gives the exact identity

\[ K_{i+1,j+1} - K_{i+1,j} - K_{i,j+1} + K_{i,j} = M_{ij}\cdot\overline{K}_{\text{cell}} . \]

Approximating the cell mean \(\overline K\) by the average of the four corners gives the implicit trapezoidal scheme implemented in SignatureKernel.solve_goursat_pde:

\[ K_{i+1,j+1} = \frac{K_{i+1,j} + K_{i,j+1} - K_{i,j} + \tfrac14 M_{ij}\,(K_{i,j}+K_{i+1,j}+K_{i,j+1})}{1 - \tfrac14 M_{ij}} . \]

The scheme is second-order accurate. For one-dimensional linear paths \(X_t = Y_t = t\) the exact kernel is \(\sum_k 1/(k!)^2 = I_0(2)\). The solver gives \(2.33\) on a single cell, \(2.27994\) on 10 cells and \(2.2795888\) on 100 cells, against \(I_0(2) = 2.2795853\). For coarse samples with large increments, refine the paths dyadically before solving.

docs.title: 3.2 Derived quantities
docs.text:
• Gram matrices. compute_gram_matrix(paths) returns \(G_{ij} = K(X^{(i)}, X^{(j)})\). \(G\) is positive semi-definite, so it can be used directly in kernel ridge regression, SVMs, MMD two-sample tests and Gaussian processes on path space.
  • Feature-space distance. normalized_distance(X, Y) returns $\(\|S(X)-S(Y)\| = \sqrt{K(X,X) - 2K(X,Y) + K(Y,Y)} .\)$ This is a metric on tree-like equivalence classes of paths.
import numpy as np
from spxa.signature import PathSignature, SignatureKernel

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.1, (30, 2)), axis=0)
y = np.cumsum(rng.normal(0, 0.1, (40, 2)), axis=0)

ps = PathSignature(depth=10)
truncated = ps.flatten_signature(ps.signature(x)) @ ps.flatten_signature(ps.signature(y))
print(truncated, SignatureKernel.evaluate(x, y))   # agree to ~1e-4 relative

docs.title: 3.3 Expected signature and linear pricing
docs.text:
Universality (§1.3) means a path-dependent payoff can be approximated as \(F(X) \approx \langle \ell, S^{(M)}(\hat X)\rangle\). Expectation is linear, so

\[ \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[F(X)] \approx \big\langle \ell,\ \mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[S^{(M)}(\hat X)]\big\rangle . \]

Once the expected signature has been computed from simulated or model paths (ExpectedSignatureNode), pricing any payoff in the span reduces to a dot product (SignatureLinearPricerNode). The weights \(\ell\) are fitted by regression on sample paths. Under mild conditions the expected signature characterises the law of the path (Chevyrev & Lyons 2016).

docs.title: 4. Relation to rough paths
docs.text: For Brownian paths and other paths with finite \(p\)-variation, \(p \in [2,3)\), the iterated integrals at level 2 are not defined pathwise. Lyons' theory makes them so by lifting \(X\) to a rough path \((X, \mathbb{X})\), where \(\mathbb{X}_{s,t}\) plays the role of \(S^{(2)}_{s,t}\) and Chen's identity is imposed as an axiom. Solutions of rough differential equations then depend continuously on the lift. For Brownian motion the Stratonovich lift \(\mathbb{X}^{ij}_{s,t} = \int_s^t (W^i_u - W^i_s)\circ dW^j_u\) is the limit of the signatures of piecewise-linear interpolations. This limit is exactly what PathSignature computes on sampled data. The antisymmetric part of \(\mathbb{X}\) is the Lévy area, the level-2 log-signature coordinate above.

docs.title: Rough Volatility
docs.text:
Time series of realised volatility behave locally like fractional Brownian motion with Hurst exponent \(H \approx 0.1\), far below the Brownian value \(H = 1/2\) (Gatheral, Jaisson & Rosenbaum 2018). Implied volatility surfaces show the matching signature: the at-the-money skew grows like \(\tau^{H-1/2}\) as maturity \(\tau \to 0\). Classical Markovian stochastic volatility models cannot produce that power law. spxa.rough implements the two reference rough models, rough Bergomi and rough Heston, together with the fractional kernels they are built on.

Object Implementation Power kernels, fBM and Volterra simulation spxa.rough.FractionalKernel Rough Bergomi model spxa.rough.RoughBergomi Rough Heston fractional Riccati solver spxa.rough.FractionalRiccatiSolver Graph nodes spxa.graph.rough.RoughKernelNode, RoughBergomiNode, FractionalRiccatiNode JAX-differentiable variants spxa.diff.simulate_diff_fbm, spxa.diff.simulate_diff_rough_heston

docs.title: 1.1 Fractional Brownian motion
docs.text:
Fractional Brownian motion \(B^H\) is the centred Gaussian process with covariance

\[ \mathbb{E}[B^H_s B^H_t] = \tfrac12\left(s^{2H} + t^{2H} - |t-s|^{2H}\right),\qquad H\in(0,1). \]

It has stationary increments and is self-similar (\(B^H_{ct} \overset{d}{=} c^H B^H_t\)). Its paths are Hölder continuous of every order below \(H\). For \(H < 1/2\) the increments are negatively correlated, and \(B^H\) is neither a semimartingale nor Markov. FractionalKernel.sample_fbm_cholesky samples it exactly on a grid by Cholesky factorisation of this covariance, at \(O(n^3)\) cost.

docs.title: 1.2 Riemann–Liouville (Volterra) processes
docs.text:
Rough volatility models are driven by the Volterra process

\[ \tilde W_t = \int_0^t (t-s)^{H-1/2}\, dZ_s, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\tilde W_t) = \frac{t^{2H}}{2H}, \]

where \(Z\) is a standard Brownian motion. \(\tilde W\) has the same local roughness and scaling as fBM but no longer has stationary increments. What makes it convenient is that it is adapted to \(Z\), so it can be correlated with the Brownian motion that drives the asset price. The joint law of \((\tilde W, Z)\) on a grid is Gaussian, with

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cov}(\tilde W_s, \tilde W_t) &= \frac{s^{a+1}\,t^{a}}{a+1}\;{}_2F_1\!\Big(-a,\,1;\,a+2;\,\tfrac{s}{t}\Big), \qquad s\le t,\ a = H-\tfrac12, \\ \operatorname{Cov}(\tilde W_t, Z_s) &= \frac{t^{a+1} - \big(t-\min(s,t)\big)^{a+1}}{a+1}, \\ \operatorname{Cov}(Z_s, Z_t) &= \min(s,t). \end{aligned} \]

The first line follows from writing \(\int_0^s (s-u)^a (t-u)^a\,du\) as an Euler integral. At \(s=t\) the hypergeometric series converges because \(c-a-b = 2H > 0\). FractionalKernel.volterra_joint_covariance assembles the \(2n\times 2n\) matrix and sample_volterra_cholesky samples it exactly (Bayer, Friz & Gatheral 2016, §4). The test suite checks every entry against direct quadrature.

docs.title: 1.3 Hybrid convolution
docs.text:
FractionalKernel.hybrid_convolution(dw, dt, b_cutoff) evaluates \(\int_0^{t_i}(t_i-s)^{H-1/2}dW_s\) from a given sequence of Brownian increments in \(O(n^2)\):

  • On the \(b\) cells nearest the singularity, it uses the exact cell-average of the kernel, \(\frac{1}{\Delta}\int_{(k-1)\Delta}^{k\Delta} s^{a}\,ds\).
  • On the remaining cells it uses the kernel value at the cell's left endpoint (a Riemann sum).

On the singular cells this is the conditional expectation of the Wiener integral given the increment. That is the best estimate available from dw alone, but it misses the variance of the residual. For \(H = 0.1\) and \(\Delta = 0.01\) it captures about 85% of the true variance \(t^{2H}/2H\). The full Bennedsen–Lunde–Pakkanen (2017) hybrid scheme recovers the missing part by sampling the local Wiener integrals jointly with \(dW\). When exact distributional properties matter, use sample_volterra_cholesky, which is what RoughBergomi does.

docs.title: 2. Rough Bergomi
docs.text:
Bayer, Friz & Gatheral (2016) model the forward variance curve \(\xi_0(t) = \mathbb{E}[v_t]\) as a lognormal Volterra functional:

\[ \begin{aligned} v_t &= \xi_0(t)\,\exp\!\Big(\eta\sqrt{2H}\,\tilde W_t - \tfrac12\eta^2 t^{2H}\Big),\\ \frac{dS_t}{S_t} &= \sqrt{v_t}\,dW_t,\qquad dW_t = \rho\,dZ_t + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,dZ^\perp_t . \end{aligned} \]

Because \(\operatorname{Var}(\sqrt{2H}\tilde W_t) = t^{2H}\), the exponential is a mean-one lognormal, so \(\mathbb{E}[v_t] = \xi_0(t)\) holds exactly. RoughBergomi uses a flat curve \(\xi_0(t) \equiv \xi_0\).

docs.title: 2.1 Simulation
docs.text:
RoughBergomi.simulate_paths proceeds in three steps:

  1. Sample \((\tilde W_{t_i}, Z_{t_i})_{i\le n}\) jointly and exactly (§1.2).
  2. Set \(v_{t_i} = \xi_0\exp(\eta\sqrt{2H}\,\tilde W_{t_i} - \tfrac12\eta^2 t_i^{2H})\). This is exact on the grid.
  3. Advance \(\log S\) with a left-point (Itô) Euler step, using \(\Delta W_i = \rho\,\Delta Z_i + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}\,\Delta Z^\perp_i\) where \(\Delta Z_i\) are the increments of the same \(Z\) that drives \(\tilde W\).

Step 3 is what produces the leverage effect: with \(\rho < 0\), returns and variance are negatively correlated. The model has no Markovian state, and exact simulation costs \(O(n^3)\) for the factorisation and \(O(n^2)\) per path. Moderate grids (\(n \lesssim 500\)) are therefore the intended use.

docs.title: 2.2 Short-time ATM skew
docs.text:
To first order in the vol-of-vol, the ATM implied volatility skew is (Fukasawa 2017; Bayer, Friz & Gatheral 2016)

\[ \left.\frac{\partial\sigma_{BS}(k,\tau)}{\partial k}\right|_{k=0} \;\approx\; \frac{\rho\,\eta\,\sqrt{2H}}{2\,(H+\tfrac12)(H+\tfrac32)}\;\tau^{H-1/2}, \qquad \tau\to0 . \]

RoughBergomi.theoretical_short_time_skew(tau) returns the absolute value of this expression. The \(1/(H+\tfrac32)\) factor is the rough-volatility counterpart of the "one-half rule" relating implied and local volatility skews (Bourgey, De Marco, Friz & Pigato 2023). In the test suite, a Monte Carlo estimate of the skew with \(H=0.1\), \(\eta=0.5\), \(\rho=-0.7\), \(\tau = 0.1\) agrees with the asymptotic formula to within about 5–10%. At 60,000 paths the Monte Carlo error dominates, and the test allows 15%.

from spxa.rough import RoughBergomi

model = RoughBergomi(hurst=0.1, eta=1.9, rho=-0.9, xi0=0.04, s0=100.0)
sim = model.simulate_paths(t_mat=1.0, n_steps=100, n_paths=20_000, seed=1)
v, s = sim["variance_paths"], sim["spot_paths"]
print(v.mean(axis=0)[[25, 50, 100]])   # ≈ 0.04 at every date (flat forward variance)
print(s[:, -1].mean())                 # ≈ 100 (martingale)

docs.title: 3. Rough Heston
docs.text:
El Euch & Rosenbaum (2019) introduced a rough version of the Heston model. Let \(\alpha = H + frac12 \in ( frac12, 1]\) and \(X_t = \log(S_t/S_0)\):

\[ egin{aligned} dX_t &= - frac12 V_t\,dt + \sqrt{V_t}\,dW_t,\ V_t &= V_0 + rac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)}\int_0^t (t-s)^{\alpha-1}\Big[\lambda( heta - V_s)\,ds + u\sqrt{V_s}\,dB_s\Big], \qquad d\langle W,B angle_t = ho\,dt . \end{aligned} \]

The model is no longer Markov, but it remains affine. Its characteristic function is

\[ \log\mathbb{E} ig[e^{iuX_T} ig] = \lambda heta\,I^1 h(u,T) + V_0\,I^{1-\alpha}h(u,T), \]

where \(I^ eta f(t) = rac{1}{\Gamma( eta)}\int_0^t (t-s)^{ eta-1}f(s)\,ds\) is the Riemann–Liouville fractional integral and \(h\) solves the fractional Riccati equation

\[ D^\alpha h = F(u,h),\qquad I^{1-\alpha}h(0) = 0, \qquad F(u,h) = - frac12(u^2 + iu) + (i ho u u - \lambda)\,h + frac12 u^2 h^2, \]

or equivalently the Volterra integral equation \(h = I^\alpha F(u,h)\).

docs.title: 3.1 Numerical solution
docs.text:
FractionalRiccatiSolver.solve integrates \(h = I^\alpha F(u,h)\) with the fractional Adams–Bashforth–Moulton predictor–corrector of Diethelm, Ford & Freed (2002). On a uniform grid \(t_k = k\Delta\), the predictor is

\[ h^P_{n} = \frac{\Delta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha+1)}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} b_{j,n}\,F(u,h_j), \qquad b_{j,n} = (n-j)^\alpha - (n-1-j)^\alpha, \]

and the corrector is

\[ h_{n} = \frac{\Delta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha+2)}\Big(F(u,h^P_{n}) + \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} a_{j,n}\,F(u,h_j)\Big), \]

with the standard product-trapezoidal weights \(a_{0,n} = (n-1)^{\alpha+1} - (n-1-\alpha)\,n^\alpha\) and \(a_{j,n} = (n-j+1)^{\alpha+1} - 2(n-j)^{\alpha+1} + (n-j-1)^{\alpha+1}\).

docs.title: 3.2 Characteristic function without singular quadrature
docs.text:
The term \(I^{1-\alpha}h\) has a weakly singular kernel. Fractional integrals form a semigroup (\(I^{\beta}I^{\gamma} = I^{\beta+\gamma}\)), and \(h = I^\alpha F\), so

\[ I^{1-\alpha}h = I^{1-\alpha}I^{\alpha}F = I^1 F(u,h) = \int_0^T F(u,h(s))\,ds . \]

rough_heston_char_func therefore evaluates

\[ \log\phi(u,T) = \lambda\theta\int_0^T h(u,s)\,ds + V_0\int_0^T F\big(u,h(u,s)\big)\,ds \]

with the trapezoidal rule. Both integrands are regular, so no singular quadrature is needed. The implementation has three consistency checks:

  • Classical limit. At \(H = \tfrac12\) (\(\alpha = 1\)), \(I^{0}h = h\) and the Riccati equation becomes the Heston ODE \(\psi' = F(u,\psi)\). The solver matches the closed-form Heston characteristic function (spxa.zoo.beyond.heston.HestonProcess.char_func) to about \(10^{-7}\) with 400 steps.
  • Martingale property. At \(u = -i\), \(F(-i, 0) = 0\), so \(h \equiv 0\) and \(\phi(-i,T) = \mathbb{E}[S_T/S_0] = 1\) exactly.
  • Convergence. Results stabilise as the grid is refined, with differences below \(10^{-5}\) between 200 and 400 steps at \(H=0.1\).

Option prices follow from \(\phi\) by standard Fourier inversion, for example the Carr–Madan damped transform used in spxa.analytics.fourier or the Lewis formula.

docs.title: Stochastic Optimal Control
docs.text:
Many problems in quantitative finance are stochastic control problems: choosing a portfolio, liquidating a position, or quoting a two-sided market. A controller steers an SDE to optimise an expected criterion. spxa.control implements the dynamic-programming framework, four canonical problems with closed-form solutions, and a monotone finite-difference HJB solver for problems without them.

docs.title: 1. Dynamic programming and the HJB equation
docs.text:
A controlled diffusion \(dX_s = \mu(s,X_s,u_s)\,ds + \sigma(s,X_s,u_s)\,dW_s\) with admissible controls \(u_s\in U\) has value function

\[ V(t,x) = \inf_{u}\ \mathbb{E}\Big[\int_t^T e^{-\rho(s-t)} f(s,X_s,u_s)\,ds + e^{-\rho(T-t)}g(X_T)\ \Big|\ X_t = x\Big]. \]

Bellman's principle of optimality gives the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation

\[ \partial_t V - \rho V + \inf_{u\in U}\Big\{\mu(t,x,u)\,\partial_x V + \tfrac12\sigma^2(t,x,u)\,\partial_{xx}V + f(t,x,u)\Big\} = 0,\qquad V(T,\cdot) = g . \]

For maximisation problems, replace \(\inf\) by \(\sup\). Verification theorem: if a smooth solution exists and the pointwise minimiser \(u^*(t,x)\) gives an admissible feedback control, then \(V\) is the value function and \(u^*\) is optimal. Without classical solutions, \(V\) is the unique viscosity solution under standard comparison conditions (Crandall–Lions; Fleming & Soner 2006).

Each ControlProblem exposes drift, diffusion, running_cost, terminal_cost, optimal_control and value_function. simulate(x0, num_steps, num_paths, seed) runs an Euler–Maruyama Monte Carlo under the feedback policy \(u^*(t,X_t)\) and returns a ControlledTrajectory holding states, controls and realised discounted payoffs. Comparing mean_cost with value_function(0, x0) checks the closed form against simulation.

docs.title: 2. Linear–quadratic–Gaussian control
docs.text:
Consider linear dynamics \(dX = (AX + Bu)\,dt + C\,dW\) with quadratic cost

\[ J(u) = \mathbb{E}\Big[\int_0^T (X^\top QX + u^\top Ru)\,dt + X_T^\top M X_T\Big], \qquad Q\succeq0,\ R\succ0,\ M\succeq0 . \]

Substituting the ansatz \(V(t,x) = x^\top P(t)x + s(t)\) into the HJB equation gives the backward matrix Riccati equation

\[ -\dot P = PA + A^\top P - PBR^{-1}B^\top P + Q,\qquad P(T) = M, \]

the optimal linear feedback \(u^*(t,x) = -R^{-1}B^\top P(t)\,x\), and \(s(t) = \int_t^T \operatorname{tr}(CC^\top P(\tau))\,d\tau\). The optimal gain does not depend on the noise \(C\) (certainty equivalence). Noise only adds the constant \(s(t)\). LinearQuadraticGaussian integrates the Riccati ODE backwards. steady_state_riccati solves the continuous algebraic Riccati equation \(PA + A^\top P - PBR^{-1}B^\top P + Q = 0\), which is the \(T\to\infty\) limit when \((A,B)\) is stabilisable and \((A,Q^{1/2})\) is detectable.

docs.title: 3. Merton's portfolio problem
docs.text:
An agent with wealth \(W\) invests \(\pi_t\) in a risky asset (\(\mu\), \(\sigma\)), keeps the remainder at the risk-free rate \(r\), and consumes at rate \(c_t\):

\[ dW_t = ig[rW_t + \pi_t(\mu - r) - c_t ig]dt + \pi_t\sigma\,dB_t . \]

The agent maximises CRRA utility \(U(c) = c^{1-\gamma}/(1-\gamma)\) (\(\gamma>0\), \(\gamma eq1\)) with discount rate \( ho\) and bequest weight \(\varepsilon\):

\[ \sup_{\pi,c}\ \mathbb{E}\Big[\int_t^T e^{- ho(s-t)} rac{c_s^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma}ds + \varepsilon\,e^{- ho(T-t)} rac{W_T^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma}\Big]. \]

Homotheticity reduces the HJB equation to an ODE. Its solution (Merton 1969, 1971) is

\[ rac{\pi^*_t}{W_t} = \alpha^* = rac{\mu - r}{\gamma\sigma^2}, \qquad rac{c^*_t}{W_t} = \kappa(t) = rac{ u}{1 + (\varepsilon^{1/\gamma} u - 1)\,e^{- u(T-t)}}, \qquad V(t,W) = \kappa(t)^{-\gamma}\, rac{W^{1-\gamma}}{1-\gamma}, \]

with

\[ u = rac{ ho - (1-\gamma)\Big(r + rac{(\mu-r)^2}{2\gamma\sigma^2}\Big)}{\gamma}. \]

The Merton fraction \(\alpha^*\) is constant in both time and wealth. As \(T o\infty\), the consumption rate \(\kappa(t)\) tends to \( u\) (infinite_horizon_consumption_propensity). Well-posedness requires \( u > 0\). MertonPortfolioControl.simulate advances log-wealth (a log-Euler step), which keeps wealth strictly positive.

docs.title: 4. Almgren–Chriss optimal execution
docs.text:
The trader liquidates \(Q_0\) shares over \([0,T]\) at trading rate \(v_t = \dot q_t\). Permanent impact moves the price by \(\gamma\,v_t\,dt\) and temporary impact makes the execution price \(\tilde S_t = S_t + \eta v_t\), with \(dS_t = \gamma v_t\,dt + \sigma\,dW_t\). Minimising the mean–variance criterion \(\mathbb{E}[\text{cost}] + \lambda\operatorname{Var}[\text{cost}]\) over deterministic schedules leads to the Euler–Lagrange equation \(\ddot q = \kappa^2 q\), where

\[ \kappa = \sqrt{\frac{\lambda\sigma^2}{\eta}} \]

is the urgency. The solution is

\[ q^*(t) = Q_0\frac{\sinh(\kappa(T-t))}{\sinh(\kappa T)},\qquad v^*(t) = -Q_0\kappa\frac{\cosh(\kappa(T-t))}{\sinh(\kappa T)}. \]

The expected cost and its variance are

\[ \mathbb{E}[C] = \tfrac12\gamma Q_0^2 + \tfrac12\eta Q_0^2\kappa\,\frac{\sinh(\kappa T)\cosh(\kappa T) + \kappa T}{\sinh^2(\kappa T)}, \qquad \operatorname{Var}[C] = \sigma^2 Q_0^2\,\frac{\sinh(2\kappa T) - 2\kappa T}{4\kappa\sinh^2(\kappa T)}. \]

As \(\lambda\to0\), \(q^*\) becomes linear (TWAP, is_twap). Sweeping \(\lambda\) traces the efficient frontier of expected cost against variance (efficient_frontier).

docs.title: 5. Avellaneda–Stoikov market making
docs.text:
A dealer quotes bid and ask prices \(s - \delta^b\) and \(s + \delta^a\) around a mid-price \(dS = \sigma\,dW\). Orders arrive as Poisson processes with intensity \(\lambda(\delta) = A e^{-k\delta}\). The dealer has CARA utility with risk aversion \(\gamma\) over terminal wealth and inventory \(q\). Avellaneda & Stoikov (2008) derive the approximate solution

\[ r(s,q,t) = s - q\,\gamma\sigma^2(T-t) \qquad\text{(reservation price)}, \] \[ \delta^a + \delta^b = \gamma\sigma^2(T-t) + \frac2\gamma\ln\Big(1 + \frac\gamma k\Big) \qquad\text{(total spread)}, \] \[ \delta^{a} = \tfrac12(\delta^a+\delta^b) - q\,\gamma\sigma^2(T-t),\qquad \delta^{b} = \tfrac12(\delta^a+\delta^b) + q\,\gamma\sigma^2(T-t). \]

The quotes are centred on the reservation price, not the mid-price. A long inventory therefore shifts both quotes down, encouraging sells and discouraging buys. The spread does not depend on inventory. optimal_quotes additionally refuses to quote on the side that would exceed max_inventory. Over a step \(\Delta t\) the fill probabilities are \(1 - e^{-\lambda(\delta)\Delta t}\) (fill_probabilities). simulate runs the joint mid-price, fill and inventory dynamics.

docs.title: 6. Finite-difference HJB solver
docs.text:
FiniteDifferenceHJB solves one-dimensional problems of the form in §1 on a grid \(x_i = x_{\min} + i\,\Delta x\), \(t_n = n\,\Delta t\), marching backwards from \(V^N = g\):

\[ V^{n}_i = V^{n+1}_i + \Delta t\Big(\operatorname*{opt}_{u\in\mathcal{U}_h}\big\{\mu\,D^{\pm}V^{n+1}_i + \tfrac12\sigma^2 D^2 V^{n+1}_i + f\big\} - \rho\,V^{n+1}_i\Big), \]

where:

  • \(D^{+}\) (forward difference) is used where \(\mu\ge0\) and \(D^{-}\) (backward difference) where \(\mu<0\) (upwinding);
  • \(D^2\) is the central second difference;
  • \(\mathcal{U}_h\) is a finite set of candidate controls (control_candidates), searched exhaustively at every node.

The scheme is explicit and monotone whenever the CFL-type condition

\[ \Delta t\left(\frac{|\mu|}{\Delta x} + \frac{\sigma^2}{\Delta x^2} + \rho\right) \le 1 \]

holds over all grid points and controls. Monotonicity, stability and consistency together imply convergence to the viscosity solution (Barles & Souganidis 1991). The solver does not enforce this condition. Choose n_time large enough, or the scheme can oscillate and diverge. Boundary nodes use Neumann (zero-gradient) or Dirichlet conditions. value(t, x) and optimal_control(t, x) interpolate the solution off-grid. For a ControlProblem instance, solve_problem(problem) reads the drift, diffusion and costs directly from the problem. The closed-form problems above serve as regression tests for the numerical solver.

docs.title: Triplet Arithmetic Under Composition
docs.text: This document derives the triplet rules that underpin spxa's operator overloading. Every formula here has a direct code counterpart in spxa/ops/.

docs.title: Addition of independent Lévy processes
docs.text:
Theorem (Sato 1999, Proposition 11.10). Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be independent Lévy processes on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with triplets \((b_X, \Sigma_X, u_X)\) and \((b_Y, \Sigma_Y, u_Y)\) respectively. Then \(Z = X + Y\) is a Lévy process with triplet

\[b_Z = b_X + b_Y, \quad \Sigma_Z = \Sigma_X + \Sigma_Y, \quad u_Z = u_X + u_Y\]

Proof sketch. The characteristic exponent is additive: \(\psi_Z(u) = \psi_X(u) + \psi_Y(u)\), which follows directly from independence and the definition of the characteristic function. Reading off the triplet components from the Lévy–Khintchine form of \(\psi_X + \psi_Y\) gives the result.

This is the core fact that makes spxa's X + Y exact. No approximation is involved for independent Lévy processes.

docs.title: Scalar multiplication
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(X\) has triplet \((b, \sigma^2, u)\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}\), then \(Z = cX\) has triplet

\[b_Z = cb + \int_{\mathbb{R}} x\left(\mathbf{1}_{\|x\| \leq 1} - \mathbf{1}_{\|cx'\| \leq 1} ight) u(dx'/c), \quad \sigma^2_Z = c^2 \sigma^2, \quad u_Z(B) = u(B/c)\]

In the one-dimensional case with the standard truncation, the drift transforms as

\[b_Z = cb + \int_1^{1/|c|} x\, \mathrm{sgn}(c)\, u(dx) \cdot \mathbf{1}_{|c| eq 1}\]

when \(|c| < 1\), and symmetrically when \(|c| > 1\). The image measure \( u_Z(B) = u(B/c)\) is exact in all cases.

Derivation. The characteristic function of \(cX_t\) is \(\mathbb{E}[e^{iucX_t}] = e^{t\psi_X(cu)}\). Substituting \(cu\) for \(u\) in the Lévy–Khintchine formula and changing variables \(x \mapsto x/c\) in the integral gives the result.

docs.title: Linear transformation
docs.text:
Theorem. If \(X\) is a \(d\)-dimensional Lévy process with triplet \((b, \Sigma, u)\) and \(A : \mathbb{R}^d o \mathbb{R}^k\) is a linear map, then \(Z = AX\) is a \(k\)-dimensional Lévy process with triplet

\[b_Z = Ab + \int_{\mathbb{R}^d} \left(Ax\, \mathbf{1}_{\|Ax\| \leq 1} - Ax\, \mathbf{1}_{\|x\| \leq 1} ight) u(dx), \quad \Sigma_Z = A\Sigma A^ op, \quad u_Z = u \circ A^{-1}\]

where \(( u \circ A^{-1})(B) = u(A^{-1}(B))\) is the image measure.

docs.title: Subordination
docs.text:
Definition. Let \(X = (X_t)_{t \geq 0}\) be a Lévy process on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) (the parent process) and \(T = (T_t)_{t \geq 0}\) be an independent subordinator — a non-decreasing Lévy process with \(T_0 = 0\). The subordinated process is \(Z_t = X_{T_t}\).

A subordinator has Laplace exponent \(\phi(\lambda) = -\log \mathbb{E}[e^{-\lambda T_1}]\), which is a Bernstein function: \(\phi(\lambda) = \delta \lambda + \int_0^\infty (1 - e^{-\lambda s})\, \rho(ds)\) with \(\delta \geq 0\) and \(\rho\) the Lévy measure of \(T\) (a measure on \((0, \infty)\) with \(\int (1 \wedge s)\, \rho(ds) < \infty\)).

Theorem (Sato 1999, Theorem 30.1; Cont & Tankov 2004, Proposition 4.4). \(Z = X \circ T\) is a Lévy process with characteristic exponent

\[\psi_Z(u) = -\phi(-\psi_X(u)) = \delta \psi_X(u) + \int_0^\infty \left(e^{s\psi_X(u)} - 1\right) \rho(ds)\]

The triplet of \(Z\) in one dimension is:

\[b_Z = \delta b_X + \int_0^\infty \left(\int_{\mathbb{R}} x\, e^{s\psi_X}\, \text{(via inversion)}\right) \rho(ds)\]

In practice, computing the triplet of \(Z\) explicitly requires either a closed-form inversion (available for named process pairs like BM-under-Gamma = Variance Gamma) or numerical evaluation of the Lévy measure via

\[\nu_Z(B) = \delta \nu_X(B) + \int_0^\infty P(X_s \in B)\, \rho(ds)\]

spxa computes subordination exactly for known pairs (documented per process) and falls back to numerical quadrature otherwise, with ExactnessLevel.MOMENT_PROPAGATION and an explicit warning.

The @ operator in spxa. Z = X @ T denotes subordination: \(Z_t = X_{T_t}\). The left operand is the parent process, the right operand must be a subordinator.

docs.title: Cumulant propagation under composition
docs.text:
For any operation producing a Lévy process, cumulants follow from the triplet:

\[\kappa_n(Z_t) = t \cdot \kappa_n(Z_1) = t \cdot \int x^n\, \nu_Z(dx) + t \cdot \sigma_Z^2 \cdot \mathbf{1}_{n=2}\]

This is computed symbolically by spxa when \(\nu_Z\) has a closed-form density, and numerically otherwise with a stated error bound.

docs.title: Property propagation
docs.text:
Operations propagate properties through the lattice defined in spxa/core/properties.py. Key rules:

Property Under \(X + Y\) Under \(cX\) Under \(X \circ T\) Stationary increments preserved preserved preserved Independent increments preserved preserved preserved Finite variance preserved if both have it preserved depends on \(T\) Finite mean preserved if both have it preserved preserved if \(T\) has finite mean Self-similarity index \(H\) lost unless \(X = Y\) preserved lost in general Martingale preserved if both are preserved if \(c \neq 0\) and \(b=0\) depends Tail index \(\alpha\) \(\min(\alpha_X, \alpha_Y)\) preserved depends on \(T\)

Cells marked "depends" cause spxa to check the specific triplet values rather than propagating symbolically.

docs.title: What breaks outside the Lévy regime
docs.text:
The above arithmetic is exact only for independent Lévy processes. The following cases require approximation:

  • Fractional Brownian motion: not a semimartingale, not a Lévy process, no triplet. The Hurst index \(H\) is the relevant parameter; self-similarity and long memory are propagated heuristically.
  • Products \(X \cdot Y\): not a Lévy process in general even for Lévy \(X\), \(Y\). spxa computes moments of the product when \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent using the moment product formula.
  • Stochastic integrals \(\int f(X_s)\, dY_s\): exact only for deterministic \(f\); for random integrands, Itô isometry gives the variance and spxa propagates moments only.

In all approximate cases, ExactnessLevel is set to MOMENT_PROPAGATION or SIMULATION_ONLY, and calling .triplet raises ExactnessError with an explanation.

docs.text:

  • Cont, R. & Tankov, P. (2004). Financial Modelling with Jump Processes. Chapman & Hall/CRC. Propositions 4.1, 4.4.
  • Schilling, R., Song, R. & Vondraček, Z. (2012). Bernstein Functions, 2nd ed. De Gruyter. Chapters 3, 5.

docs.title: Tutorial 1 — First Composition¶
docs.text: This notebook introduces the core idea of spxa: stochastic processes as first-class algebraic objects. You write Z = X + c*Y or W = X @ T and get back a new process with exact analytical properties.

docs.title: 1. Adding two processes¶
docs.text: For independent Lévy processes $X$ and $Y$, the sum $Z = X + Y$ has triplet $$ (b_Z, \sigma^2_Z, u_Z) = (b_X + b_Y,\; \sigma^2_X + \sigma^2_Y,\; u_X + u_Y) $$ This is exact — not an approximation.

docs.title: 2. Scalar multiplication¶
docs.text: For $Z = c \cdot X$, the triplet transforms as $$ (b_Z, \sigma^2_Z, \nu_Z) = (cb + \Delta b,\; c^2 \sigma^2,\; \nu(\cdot/c)) $$ The drift correction $\Delta b$ accounts for mass shifting across the unit ball under the truncation function.

docs.title: 3. Cumulant table¶
docs.text: Every EXACT process exposes analytical cumulants via the Lévy–Khintchine formula. The cumulant table also computes skewness and excess kurtosis.

docs.title: 4. Subordination¶
docs.text: Subordinating Brownian motion by a Gamma process gives the Variance Gamma model. The @ operator does this: W = BM @ Gamma.

docs.title: 5. The Story: derivation trace¶
docs.text: .__story__() produces a human-readable derivation of how the current process was constructed.

docs.title: 6. LaTeX rendering (Jupyter only)¶
docs.text: In a Jupyter environment, you can render the derivation as LaTeX:

docs.title: 7. Property lattice¶
docs.text: Properties propagate automatically. The library is honest when they are lost.

docs.title: Tutorial 2 — Finance Models¶
docs.text:
spxa is purpose-built for quantitative finance. This notebook covers:

  • Exponential Lévy models for asset prices
  • European option pricing via the Carr-Madan FFT method
  • Implied volatility smile from VG and NIG models
  • Comparing models via Hellinger and L² distances

docs.title: 1. Geometric Lévy models¶
docs.text: The exponential Lévy model is $S_t = S_0 \exp(rt + X_t)$ where $X$ is a Lévy process. The risk-neutral drift is chosen so $\mathbb{E}[S_t] = S_0 e^{rt}$.

docs.title: 2. European option pricing — Carr-Madan FFT¶
docs.text: For a Lévy log-return process $X$ with characteristic function $\phi(u;t)$, the call price is given by the Carr-Madan formula: $$ C(K) = \frac{e^{-\alpha k}}{\pi} \int_0^\infty e^{-iuk} \psi(u)\, du $$ where $k = \log(K/S_0)$ and $\psi$ is a modified version of $\phi$.

docs.title: 3. Cumulant comparison¶
docs.text: The cumulants directly encode the shape of the distribution — skewness and kurtosis are why Lévy models produce smiles.

docs.title: 4. Model distances¶
docs.text: spxa computes L² and Hellinger distances between marginal distributions directly from the characteristic functions — no Monte Carlo needed.

docs.title: 5. Stochastic volatility via subordination¶
docs.text: The Variance Gamma model is exactly a BM subordinated by a Gamma process. The subordinator acts as a stochastic clock — business time vs calendar time.

docs.title: Tutorial 3 — Physics Applications¶
docs.text:
Lévy processes appear throughout statistical physics:

  • Anomalous diffusion — fractional BM and α-stable processes
  • First passage times — exact Lévy distribution
  • Stochastic volatility via subordination — random time changes
  • Hawkes processes — self-exciting point processes in neuroscience and seismology

docs.title: 1. Anomalous diffusion: fractional Brownian motion¶
docs.text:
Standard BM has $\text{Var}(B_t) = \sigma^2 t$ (linear in $t$). Fractional BM with Hurst index $H$ has $$\text{Var}(B^H_t) = \sigma^2 t^{2H}$$

  • $H = 0.5$: standard diffusion (Brownian)
  • $H > 0.5$: superdiffusion (long memory, persistent increments)
  • $H < 0.5$: subdiffusion (anti-persistent increments)

docs.title: 2. Mean-square displacement¶
docs.text: MSD$(t) = \mathbb{E}[|X_t - X_0|^2]$ is a key observable in single-particle tracking experiments. For fBM: MSD$(t) = 2\sigma^2 t^{2H}$.

docs.title: 3. Heavy-tailed diffusion: α-stable processes¶
docs.text: For $\alpha < 2$, the $\alpha$-stable process has power-law tails: no finite variance, no finite mean for $\alpha \leq 1$. This describes Lévy flights observed in animal foraging, plasma turbulence, and financial returns.

docs.title: 4. First passage times¶
docs.text: The time for BM to hit a level $a > 0$ follows the Lévy distribution: $$P(\tau \leq t) = 2\Phi(-a/(\sigma\sqrt{t}))$$ This is an $\alpha=1/2$ stable distribution — heavy-tailed with infinite mean.

docs.title: 5. Hawkes process — self-exciting events¶
docs.text: The Hawkes process models event clustering: each event increases the probability of future events. Applications: earthquake aftershocks, neural spike trains, high-frequency order book arrivals.

docs.title: 6. OU-Lévy — stochastic volatility¶
docs.text: The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process driven by a Gamma subordinator is the Barndorff-Nielsen–Shephard stochastic volatility model. The variance process $V_t$ is stationary, non-negative, and mean-reverting.
